pra.name: Pre-Prophethood
pra.desc: Arabia before prophethood: the Ka'bah, Quraysh, Year of the Elephant, and key figures around the Prophet's birth.

makkah.name: Mecca Period
makkah.desc: First revelation, secret and public preaching, Quraysh persecution, and migration to Abyssinia.

madinah.name: Medina Period
madinah.desc: The Hijrah and Medina state, battles from Badr to Khandaq, Hudaybiyyah, Fathu Makkah, and the Prophet's passing.

khulafaur.name: Khulafaur Rasyidin
khulafaur.desc: The first four caliphs—Abu Bakar, Umar, Utsman, and Ali—expanding across Syria, Persia, and Egypt.

umayyah.name: Umayyad Caliphate
umayyah.desc: Governance from Damascus, expansion into Andalusia and Sindh, and the birth of monumental Islamic architecture.

abbasiyah.name: Abbasid Golden Age
abbasiyah.desc: Baghdad as a global center of scholarship, translation, and science alongside Cordoba and Fatimid Cairo.

seljuk.name: Seljuk, Crusades & Mongols
seljuk.desc: Seljuk rise, the Crusades, Salahuddin al-Ayyubi, and the Mongol sack of Baghdad.

mamluk.name: Mamluk & Post-Mongol
mamluk.desc: Mamluks halting the Mongols at Ain Jalut, Ottoman rise, fall of Granada, and Nusantara sultanates.

imperium.name: Three Gunpowder Empires
imperium.desc: Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal empires at their peak while Nusantara sultanates confronted the VOC.

kolonial.name: Colonialism & Reform
kolonial.desc: The Muslim world facing European colonialism, reformist movements, and the abolition of the caliphate.

modern.name: Modern Era
modern.desc: Nation-states, independence movements, modern Islamic organizations, and contemporary geopolitical shifts.

makkah.name: Mecca
makkah.subtitle: Birthplace of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ
makkah.description: Commercial and spiritual hub of the Arabian Peninsula where the Ka'bah stands under Quraysh guardianship.

yatsrib.name: Yathrib (Medina)
yatsrib.subtitle: Oasis north of Mecca
yatsrib.description: Fertile oasis inhabited by Aws, Khazraj, and Jewish tribes; became the destination of the Hijrah in 622 CE.

syam.name: Syam (Levant)
syam.subtitle: Quraysh caravan destination
syam.description: Northern trade route of Quraysh caravans where young Muhammad met monk Bahira in Busra.

palestina.name: Palestine
palestina.subtitle: Land of Baitul Maqdis
palestina.description: Region housing Masjid al-Aqsa, the first Qibla of Muslims before Mecca.

iraq.name: Iraq (Ancient)
iraq.subtitle: Under Sassanid Persian sphere
iraq.description: Region under the Sassanid Empire before the campaigns of Qadisiyyah and the founding of Kufah.

yaman.name: Yemen
yaman.subtitle: Domain of Abrahah
yaman.description: Southern Arabian territory governed by Abrahah on behalf of the Aksumite Kingdom.

gajah.name: Route of the Elephant Army
gajah.subtitle: Yemen toward Mecca, c. 570 CE
gajah.description: Campaign route of Abrahah's army marching toward Mecca before perishing outside the sanctuary.

hira.name: Cave of Hira
hira.subtitle: Jabal al-Nour, near Mecca
hira.description: Mountain cave where Prophet Muhammad ﷺ retreated in contemplation and received the first revelation in 610 CE.

makkah-k.name: Mecca
makkah-k.subtitle: Sanctuary of the Ka'bah
makkah-k.description: Opened nearly without bloodshed during Fathu Makkah (8 AH / 630 CE), remaining the center of Hajj.

madinah-k.name: Medina
madinah-k.subtitle: First capital of the Islamic state
madinah-k.description: Seat of governance from the Hijrah through the era of Utsman; home to the Prophet's Mosque.

badar.name: Badr
badar.subtitle: Valley of the first major battle
badar.description: Site of the Battle of Badr (17 Ramadan 2 AH / 624 CE), where 313 Muslims defeated a larger Quraysh force.

khaibar.name: Khaybar
khaibar.subtitle: Fortified oasis north of Medina
khaibar.description: Walled agricultural oasis captured in 7 AH / 628 CE.

tabuk.name: Tabuk
tabuk.subtitle: The Prophet's final campaign
tabuk.description: Northern frontier expedition in 9 AH / 630 CE facing Byzantine mobilization.

yamamah.name: Yamamah
yamamah.subtitle: Battlefield of the Riddah Wars
yamamah.description: Interior Najd plain where Khalid bin Walid defeated Musaylimah in 12 AH / 633 CE.

damaskus.name: Damascus
damaskus.subtitle: Capital of Syam
damaskus.description: Ancient Levantine city taken in 14 AH / 635 CE under Khalid bin Walid and Abu Ubaidah.

yarmuk.name: Yarmuk
yarmuk.subtitle: Decisive battle for Syam
yarmuk.description: Site of the 636 CE victory over Byzantine forces that opened all of Greater Syria.

baitulmaqdis.name: Baitul Maqdis
baitulmaqdis.subtitle: Jerusalem, the first Qibla
baitulmaqdis.description: Surrendered peacefully to Caliph Umar bin Khattab in 16 AH / 637 CE under a treaty protecting lives and worship.

hims.name: Homs (Hims)
hims.subtitle: Northern Syrian city
hims.description: Strategic Syrian city conquered after Yarmuk; resting place of Khalid bin Walid.

konstantinopel.name: Constantinople
konstantinopel.subtitle: Byzantine imperial capital
konstantinopel.description: Fortified capital on the Bosphorus besieged multiple times before falling in 1453 CE.

iskandariyah.name: Alexandria
iskandariyah.subtitle: Major Mediterranean port of Egypt
iskandariyah.description: Byzantine port city captured by Amr bin Ash in 21 AH / 642 CE.

fustat.name: Fustat
fustat.subtitle: First Islamic capital in Egypt
fustat.description: Garrison city founded by Amr bin Ash around 20 AH with the first mosque in Africa.

barqah.name: Barqah (Cyrenaica)
barqah.subtitle: Eastern Libya gateway
barqah.description: Region opened by Amr bin Ash around 22 AH / 643 CE on the road to North Africa.

kufah.name: Kufah & Qadisiyyah
kufah.subtitle: Iraqi garrison hub
kufah.description: Site of the 636 CE victory over Sassanid Persia, followed by Sa'ad bin Abi Waqqash founding Kufah.

madain.name: Al-Mada'in (Ctesiphon)
madain.subtitle: Sassanid imperial capital
madain.description: Persian capital captured in 16 AH / 637 CE following the Battle of Qadisiyyah.

basrah.name: Basra
basrah.subtitle: Southern Iraq garrison city
basrah.description: Port and military base founded around 14 AH; nearby site of the Battle of the Camel in 36 AH.

nahawand.name: Nahawand
nahawand.subtitle: Victory of Victories
nahawand.description: Decisive 21 AH / 642 CE battle breaking organized Sassanid resistance on the Iranian plateau.

merv.name: Merv
merv.subtitle: Eastern frontier of Khorasan
merv.description: Oasis city near which the last Sassanid ruler Yazdegerd III died in 31 AH / 651 CE.

habasyah.name: Abyssinia (Aksum)
habasyah.subtitle: First sanctuary of migration
habasyah.description: Christian kingdom in modern Ethiopia where King Negus protected early Muslim refugees in 615 CE.

mesir.name: Egypt
mesir.subtitle: Granary of the Mediterranean & Seat of Fustat and al-Azhar
mesir.description: The ancient Nile civilization opened to Islam in 639–641 CE under Amr ibn al-As, later housing al-Fustat, al-Azhar, and the Mamluk Sultanate.
mesir.facts:
Region : North Africa (Nile Valley)
Key Milestones : 640 CE Babylon Siege, 641 CE Founding of Fustat, 970 CE al-Azhar
mesir.body:
Geographical Overview & Early Islam

Bordering the Sinai corridor to the east and the Mediterranean to the north, Egypt linked the Red Sea to the Levant and North Africa. Following Amr ibn al-As's campaign of 639–641 CE, Egypt emerged as an agrarian, naval, and scholarly powerhouse, home to Fustat, Cairo, and the historic Mosque of al-Azhar.

About This Telling

Synthesized from Tarikh al-Tabari, al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, and ArchNet.

thaif.name: Ta'if
thaif.subtitle: Highland Oasis of Banu Thaqif in the Sarawat Mountains
thaif.description: Elevated fertile valleys southeast of Mecca where Banu Thaqif resided, witness to the Prophet's steadfast visit in 619 CE and later voluntary allegiance.
thaif.facts:
Region : Hijaz Highlands, Western Arabia
Key Events : 619 CE Da'wah to Ta'if, 630 CE Siege of Ta'if
thaif.body:
Highland Geography & Historical Role

Nestled above the Hijazi escarpment south of Mecca, Ta'if was renowned across Arabia for irrigated orchards, cool air, and fortified walls inhabited by Banu Thaqif. Following the Year of Sorrow in 619 CE, the city became a scene of immense forbearance before eventually embracing Islam through peaceful delegation in 9 AH.

About This Telling

Documented in Sirah Ibn Hisham and Tarikh al-Tabari.

laut-merah.name: The Red Sea
laut-merah.subtitle: Ancient Maritime Corridor Linking Hijaz, Abyssinia & Suez
laut-merah.description: The narrow maritime artery connecting Meccan ports like Shu'aybah and Jeddah with Aksumite Africa, Yemen, and Egypt.
laut-merah.facts:
Region : Between Arabian Peninsula & Northeast Africa
Key Port : Shu'aybah, Jeddah, Suez
laut-merah.body:
Maritime Significance in Islamic History

Known classically as Bahr al-Qulzum, the Red Sea connected the Hijazi ports of Shu'aybah and Jeddah directly to East Africa, Yemen, and Suez. Early Muslim emigrants sailed across its waters to Abyssinia in 615 CE, and sea trade later supplied Mecca and Medina from Egypt.

About This Telling

Compiled from Sirah Ibn Hisham and Tarikh al-Tabari.

persia.name: Persia (Iran)
persia.subtitle: Iranian Plateau of Cities, Science & Classical Scholarship
persia.description: Former heartland of the Sassanian Empire whose cities of Isfahan, Nishapur, Rayy, and Shiraz became pillars of Islamic philosophy, medicine, and hadith science.
persia.facts:
Region : Iranian Plateau
Key Cities : Hamadan, Rayy, Isfahan, Nishapur, Shiraz
persia.body:
Transformation of the Iranian Plateau

Spanning the Zagros valleys to the eastern plains of Khurasan, Persia passed from Sassanian imperial rule after Qadisiyyah (636 CE) and Nahavand (642 CE) into a vibrant center of Islamic scholarship, producing pioneering jurists, historians, and polymaths.

About This Telling

Referenced from Tarikh al-Tabari and al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh.

570-tahun-gajah.title: Year of the Elephant
570-tahun-gajah.summary: Abrahah marched from Yemen with an army led by elephants to destroy the Ka'bah. His forces perished at Wadi Muhassar before entering Makkah (QS. Al-Fil), marking the era known as the Year of the Elephant.
570-tahun-gajah.facts:
Date : Around 570 CE
Primary Location : Wadi Muhassar (between Mina and Muzdalifah, near Makkah)
Key Figures : Abrahah al-Ashram, Abdul Muthalib ibn Hashim, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami
Military Force : Expeditionary army from Yemen with war elephants (lead elephant Mahmud)
Primary Reference : Quran, Surah Al-Fil (105:1-5)
570-tahun-gajah.body:
Context & Background

In the mid-sixth century CE, southern Arabia lay under the authority of the Aksumite Kingdom of Abyssinia. Abrahah al-Ashram, the Aksumite viceroy in Yemen, erected a grand cathedral called al-Qullays in Sana'a to redirect Arab pilgrims and overland caravans away from Makkah. The project failed to draw tribes away from the Ka'bah, which remained the focal sanctuary and commercial hub of the Hijaz.

Tensions escalated when a member of the Kinanah tribe reportedly desecrated al-Qullays in protest against Abrahah's ambitions. Seeking to assert dominance over the western Arabian trade corridor, Abrahah assembled an expeditionary force around 570 CE and marched north toward Makkah accompanied by war elephants, including a prominent lead elephant named Mahmud.

Course of Events

1. March North and Early Resistance

News of the campaign spread rapidly along the Yemeni-Hijazi road. Local chieftains attempted to block the advance, notably Dhu Nafar of Himyar and Nufayl ibn Habib of Khath'am. Abrahah defeated both forces and pressed Nufayl into service as a reluctant guide toward the Hijaz.

  • Key Point: At Ta'if, the leaders of Banu Thaqif avoided confrontation and supplied Abu Righal to guide the army to the outskirts of Makkah.

2. Abdul Muthalib's Parley with Abrahah

Upon encamping at al-Mughammas near Makkah, Abrahah's vanguard seized local livestock, including two hundred camels belonging to the Quraysh elder Abdul Muthalib ibn Hashim. When Abdul Muthalib met Abrahah in camp, he requested only the return of his camels. When Abrahah expressed surprise that he did not plead for the Ka'bah, Abdul Muthalib stated calmly that the camels had an owner to defend them, whereas the Sacred House had its own Lord who would protect it.

  • Key Point: Following the parley, Abdul Muthalib evacuated the people of Makkah to the surrounding mountain slopes to avoid civilian slaughter.

3. Destruction at Wadi Muhassar

As the army prepared to enter the sanctuary valley through Wadi Muhassar, between Mina and Muzdalifah, the lead elephant Mahmud knelt and refused to move toward Makkah, even though it readily walked toward Yemen, Syria, or the east. Flocks of birds (tayran ababil) then appeared from the sea and pelted the troops with small stones of baked clay (sijjil).

  • Key Point: Disease and panic shattered the expedition; Abrahah retreated in severe physical collapse and died shortly after reaching Sana'a.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The collapse of Abrahah's campaign elevated the standing of Quraysh across Arabia as guardians of the Ka'bah. Their winter and summer caravan routes to Yemen and Greater Syria gained greater security, an outcome commemorated in Surah Al-Fil and Surah Quraysh. Hijazi communities subsequently anchored their oral chronology to this event as the Year of the Elephant.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This account draws on Surah Al-Fil (Quran.com) alongside classical Arabic chronicles: Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), al-Tabari's Tarikh ar-Rusul wal-Muluk (Shamela 23833), and Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288). The 570 CE date reflects classical Sirah consensus, while some epigraphic studies place Abrahah's northern campaigns between 552 and 571 CE.

570-kelahiran-nabi.title: Birth of the Prophet
570-kelahiran-nabi.summary: Muhammad ﷺ was born in Makkah to Aminah bint Wahb during the Year of the Elephant. His father Abdullah had passed away before his birth, leaving his grandfather Abdul Muthalib as his guardian.
570-kelahiran-nabi.facts:
Date : 570 CE (Rabi' al-Awwal, Year of the Elephant)
Primary Location : Shi'b Bani Hashim, Makkah
Parents : Abdullah ibn Abdul Muthalib & Aminah bint Wahb
Early Caregivers : Abdul Muthalib ibn Hashim and Thuwaybah
Clan : Banu Hashim (Quraysh)
570-kelahiran-nabi.body:
Context & Background

In the late 560s CE, Makkah's civic leadership centered around Abdul Muthalib ibn Hashim, who oversaw the siqayah (water provision) and rifadah (hospitality for pilgrims). His son Abdullah married Aminah bint Wahb ibn Abd Manaf of Banu Zuhrah, a respected clan within Quraysh.

Shortly after the marriage, Abdullah joined a summer trade caravan to Greater Syria. On the return journey, he fell ill and stopped at Yathrib among his maternal relatives of Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar, where he died and was buried several months before his son was born.

Course of Events

1. Birth in Shi'b Bani Hashim

Muhammad ﷺ was born in the quarter of Banu Hashim in Makkah on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal during the Year of the Elephant (c. 570 or 571 CE). Classical historians widely cite 12 Rabi' al-Awwal, while several astronomical calculations and early reports mention 9 Rabi' al-Awwal. Al-Shifa', the mother of Abdurrahman ibn Awf, attended Aminah during childbirth.

  • Key Point: Word of the birth was immediately brought to Abdul Muthalib while he was seated near the Ka'bah.

2. Supplication at the Ka'bah and Naming

Abdul Muthalib came to receive his grandson, carried him to the Ka'bah to offer prayers of gratitude to God, and returned him to Aminah. On the seventh day, he hosted a feast for the Quraysh and named the child Muhammad, a name virtually unused among Arab families of that era.

  • Key Point: When Quraysh elders asked why he departed from ancestral names, Abdul Muthalib replied that he hoped his grandson would be praised in the heavens and on earth.

3. Early Nursing in Makkah

During the first days, Aminah nursed the newborn herself. Afterward, Thuwaybah—a servant freed by Abu Lahab upon hearing news of his nephew's birth—nursed him for a brief period. Thuwaybah had previously nursed Hamzah ibn Abdul Muthalib and later nursed Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad, establishing ties of foster brotherhood.

  • Key Point: These foster kinship bonds later held direct legal and social significance in the early Muslim community.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Born an orphan within Banu Hashim, Muhammad ﷺ entered Makkan society without substantial inherited wealth from his father. His early upbringing under Abdul Muthalib linked his household to both Quraysh leadership in Makkah and maternal relatives in Yathrib, ties that proved decisive decades later during the Hijrah.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on classical Sirah sources: Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), authenticated reports on the Monday birth and foster kinship via Thuwaybah in Sunnah.com, and Ar-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Archive.org). In keeping with Islamic historical standards, no physical attributes of the Prophet ﷺ or his family are depicted.

572-disusui-siti-halimah.title: Nursed by Halimah al-Sa'diyyah
572-disusui-siti-halimah.summary: Following Quraysh custom, the infant Muhammad ﷺ was entrusted to Halimah al-Sa'diyyah in the desert settlement of Banu Sa'd so he could grow in a healthy rural climate and learn pure Arabic.
572-disusui-siti-halimah.facts:
Date : Around 570-575 CE (nursing period centered c. 572 CE)
Primary Location : Lands of Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr (Hawazin territory, Hijaz interior)
Foster Mother : Halimah bint Abi Dhu'ayb al-Sa'diyyah
Foster Father : Al-Harith ibn Abd al-Uzza al-Sa'di
Foster Siblings : Abdullah, Anisah, and Hudhafah (al-Shayma') bint al-Harith
572-disusui-siti-halimah.body:
Context & Background

Prominent Quraysh households regularly sent their infants to Bedouin wet nurses in the desert highlands so the children would grow up away from Makkah's valley fevers and acquire eloquent classical Arabic. Women from Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, a branch of the Hawazin confederation, traveled to Makkah seasonally seeking infants from affluent families.

That year, severe drought gripped the territory of Banu Sa'd, leaving pastures barren and livestock thin. Halimah bint Abi Dhu'ayb traveled to Makkah alongside her husband al-Harith ibn Abd al-Uzza and other women of her tribe in dire hardship.

Course of Events

1. Halimah Accepts the Infant Muhammad ﷺ

Each nurse from Banu Sa'd initially declined Aminah's orphan infant, expecting minimal compensation without a living father. Finding no other child before the caravan departed, Halimah consulted her husband and decided to take the orphan rather than return empty-handed.

  • Key Point: Sirah reports note that upon departing Makkah, Halimah's previously weak mount outpaced the rest of the Banu Sa'd caravan.

2. Childhood Years Among Banu Sa'd

During his stay in the desert settlement, Halimah's household experienced marked relief: their sheep returned full with abundant milk even as neighboring flocks suffered from the drought. After weaning him at age two, Halimah brought him briefly to Makkah and persuaded Aminah to let him stay longer in the desert air, citing Makkah's seasonal illnesses.

  • Key Point: Among Banu Sa'd, he grew up alongside his foster siblings Abdullah, Anisah, and al-Shayma', assisting in herding lambs around the camp.

3. The Opening of the Chest and Return to Makkah

Around age four or five, while playing behind the tents with other children, the event known as shaqq al-sadr (the opening and cleansing of the heart) occurred, as narrated in Sahih Muslim on the authority of Anas ibn Malik. Frightened by what they witnessed, the foster children ran to alert Halimah and al-Harith.

  • Key Point: Concerned for the child's safety after this extraordinary event, Halimah and al-Harith promptly returned him to his mother Aminah in Makkah.

Historical Impact & Legacy

His formative years in the desert anchored his mastery of pure Arabic speech, a heritage he later acknowledged when referencing his upbringing among Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr. He maintained lifelong respect for his foster family, honoring al-Shayma' and showing clemency to Hawazin captives decades later after the Battle of Hunayn.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This entry is drawn from the narration in Sahih Muslim via Sunnah.com, Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), and Ar-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Archive.org). All descriptions focus strictly on historical actions and kinship without physical depictions.

576-yatim-piatu.title: Orphaned at Six and Eight
576-yatim-piatu.summary: Aminah passed away at al-Abwa while returning from Yathrib in 576 CE. Two years later Abdul Muthalib died, and Abu Thalib assumed responsibility for raising the young Muhammad ﷺ.
576-yatim-piatu.facts:
Date : 576 CE (death of Aminah) and 578 CE (death of Abdul Muthalib)
Primary Location : Yathrib, al-Abwa (between Makkah and Yathrib), and Makkah
Key Figures : Aminah bint Wahb, Umm Ayman (Barakah), Abdul Muthalib, Abu Thalib
Age of the Prophet ﷺ : 6 years old (double orphan) and 8 years old (placed with Abu Thalib)
Clans Involved : Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar (Yathrib) and Banu Hashim (Makkah)
576-yatim-piatu.body:
Context & Background

After returning from Halimah al-Sa'diyyah around age five, Muhammad ﷺ lived with his mother Aminah bint Wahb in Makkah. Although orphaned of his father before birth, his family maintained kinship ties with Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar in Yathrib through his paternal grandmother Salma bint Amr.

In 576 CE, when her son was six years old, Aminah undertook the long journey from Makkah to Yathrib to visit the grave of Abdullah and introduce young Muhammad ﷺ to his relatives in the oasis.

Course of Events

1. Journey to Yathrib and Aminah's Death at al-Abwa

Aminah traveled to Yathrib with her son and their loyal servant Umm Ayman (Barakah al-Habashiyyah). They stayed for about a month among Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar. On the return road toward Makkah, Aminah fell gravely ill at al-Abwa, a stopping point roughly halfway between the two towns, where she died and was buried.

  • Key Point: Umm Ayman escorted the newly orphaned child safely back to Makkah into the care of his grandfather Abdul Muthalib.

2. Two Years Under Abdul Muthalib's Protection

Abdul Muthalib cared closely for his grandson, granting him affection beyond that shown to his own sons. A special mat was regularly spread for Abdul Muthalib in the shade of the Ka'bah where none of his sons dared sit out of deference, yet he seated young Muhammad ﷺ beside him and forbade his sons from pushing him away.

  • Key Point: This guardianship ended after two years when Abdul Muthalib died at an advanced age in 578 CE, leaving Muhammad ﷺ eight years old.

3. Custody Passes to Abu Thalib

Before passing away, Abdul Muthalib entrusted the child to Abu Thalib ibn Abdul Muthalib, because Abu Thalib and Abdullah were full brothers born to Fatimah bint Amr al-Makhzumiyyah. Abu Thalib raised his nephew alongside his own children and stood by him for more than forty years.

  • Key Point: To ease the modest household expenses of Abu Thalib, the young boy tended sheep for the people of Makkah for a few qirats of wages.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Losing both parents and his grandfather in early childhood cultivated self-reliance and deep concern for orphans and the vulnerable, themes directly addressed later in Surah Al-Duha (93:6-9). His lifelong bond with Umm Ayman and his early acquaintance with Yathrib also endured into the Madinan era.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Chronology and locations follow Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), al-Tabari's Tarikh (Shamela 23833), and Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), corroborated by hadith reports on visiting al-Abwa and herding sheep in Sunnah.com and Surah Al-Duha at Quran.com.

582-bertemu-bahira.title: Meeting the Monk Bahira
582-bertemu-bahira.summary: During a trade caravan to Syria with Abu Thalib around 582 CE, the Christian monk Bahira in Bosra recognized signs of future prophethood in young Muhammad ﷺ and urged Abu Thalib to guard him.
582-bertemu-bahira.facts:
Date : Around 582 CE
Primary Location : Bosra (southern Syria)
Key Figures : Abu Thalib ibn Abdul Muthalib, young Muhammad ﷺ (c. 12 years old), Bahira
Travel Context : Quraysh summer caravan from Makkah to Syria
Source Corpus : Classical Sirah chronicles and Jami' al-Tirmidhi
582-bertemu-bahira.body:
Context & Background

Summer overland trade to Greater Syria formed the financial backbone of Quraysh in Makkah. When his nephew reached roughly twelve years of age around 582 CE, Abu Thalib prepared a merchant caravan for the northern route. Initially, he intended to leave Muhammad ﷺ in Makkah due to the hardship of desert travel.

As the caravan prepared to depart, however, the boy showed deep distress at being separated from his guardian. Abu Thalib relented and brought him along the western Arabian trade corridor toward Bosra on the southern frontier of Syria.

Course of Events

1. Encampment at Bosra

After crossing the long Hijazi trail, the Quraysh caravan halted outside Bosra, an important commercial hub under Byzantine and Ghassanid influence. Near their resting site stood a hermitage inhabited by a learned Christian monk named Bahira, well versed in older scriptures.

  • Key Point: Sirah reports note that while Bahira had ignored passing Quraysh caravans for years, on this occasion he prepared a generous meal and invited the entire company.

2. The Feast and Bahira's Inquiry

When the merchants entered the monastery to eat, young Muhammad ﷺ remained outside guarding the baggage and camels. Scanning the guests, Bahira asked whether anyone had been left behind. Learning that a boy remained with the gear, he insisted that the boy be brought to join the meal.

  • Key Point: During the gathering, Bahira questioned the boy about his sleep, his attitude toward the idols al-Lat and al-Uzza, and examined prophetic signs known from earlier books.

3. Warning to Abu Thalib

Following the meal, Bahira spoke privately with Abu Thalib regarding his relationship to the youth. When Abu Thalib referred to him as his son, Bahira objected that the boy's father could not still be alive, prompting Abu Thalib to explain that he was his nephew. Bahira then advised Abu Thalib to send him back to Makkah and protect him from hostile factions in Syria who might harm him if they recognized the same signs.

  • Key Point: Once his commercial dealings in Bosra concluded, Abu Thalib arranged for his nephew to return safely to Makkah ahead of trouble with trusted companions.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The journey to Bosra exposed Muhammad ﷺ early in life to regional trade networks, Syrian urban markets, and Christian scholarly communities on Arabia's northern frontier. It also reinforced Abu Thalib's vigilance over his nephew's safety throughout his youth in Makkah.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

The encounter with Bahira is preserved in Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), al-Tabari's Tarikh (Shamela 23833), Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), and Jami' al-Tirmidhi via Sunnah.com, with chain evaluations on Dorar.net. Classical hadith critics such as al-Dhahabi and Ibn Kathir noted a textual insertion (idraj) in one transmission mentioning Bilal as an escort, as Bilal could not have served in that role in 582 CE.

595-menikah-dengan-khadijah.title: Marriage to Khadijah
595-menikah-dengan-khadijah.summary: After managing a profitable trade caravan to Syria for Khadijah bint Khuwaylid and earning renown across Makkah as Al-Amin, Muhammad ﷺ married her around 595 CE.
595-menikah-dengan-khadijah.facts:
Date : Around 595 CE
Primary Location : Makkah
Key Figures : Muhammad ﷺ (25 years old) & Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (Banu Asad)
Intermediaries & Witnesses : Maysarah, Nafisah bint Munyah, Abu Thalib, Waraqah ibn Nawfal
Dowry (Mahr) : 20 young camels
595-menikah-dengan-khadijah.body:
Context & Background

By the mid-590s CE, Muhammad ﷺ had earned widespread respect in Makkah through his participation in the Hilf al-Fudul pact for civic justice and his commercial partnerships with Quraysh merchants such as al-Sa'ib ibn Abi al-Sa'ib. His strict honesty in handling deposits and contracts won him the title Al-Amin (the Trustworthy).

Meanwhile, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid ibn Asad of Banu Asad was a prominent and wealthy merchant in Makkah. Rather than leading overland caravans herself, she routinely entrusted her capital to reliable Quraysh agents under profit-sharing agreements.

Course of Events

1. Commercial Expedition to Syria with Maysarah

Having learned of his integrity, Khadijah offered Muhammad ﷺ double her usual commission to lead a trade caravan to the market of Bosra in Syria. He accepted and departed accompanied by her trusted attendant, Maysarah.

  • Key Point: Trade in Bosra yielded exceptional profits, and throughout the return trip Maysarah carefully observed his partner's honesty and composure.

2. Maysarah's Report and Marriage Proposal

Upon reaching Makkah, the entire proceeds were handed over to Khadijah alongside Maysarah's detailed account of the journey. After consulting her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, Khadijah asked her friend Nafisah bint Munyah to approach Muhammad ﷺ discreetly and inquire about his readiness for marriage.

  • Key Point: Once he agreed, both extended families arranged the formal betrothal and marriage contract.

3. The Marriage Contract in Makkah

About two months after the caravan's return in 595 CE, elders of Banu Hashim led by Abu Thalib and Hamzah ibn Abdul Muthalib visited Banu Asad to present the proposal before Khadijah's guardian (cited as her uncle Amr ibn Asad in major reports). Abu Thalib delivered the formal marriage address before leaders of both clans, setting a dowry of twenty young camels.

  • Key Point: Their union produced six children: Qasim, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, and Abdullah.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The marriage established a stable household in Makkah that lasted twenty-five years until Khadijah's death. Her moral counsel, steadfastness, and material backing proved indispensable when the first revelation arrived fifteen years later, making her the first person to embrace the message of Islam.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Historical details follow Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), al-Tabari's Tarikh (Shamela 23833), Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), and al-Dhahabi's Siyar A'lam an-Nubala' (Shamela 23680). Classical sources predominantly report Khadijah's age at marriage as forty, though minor variations between twenty-eight and forty appear in early biographical compilations. No physical descriptions are included, adhering to Islamic standards of honor.

605-peletakan-hajar-aswad.title: Placement of the Black Stone
605-peletakan-hajar-aswad.summary: During the 605 CE reconstruction of the Ka'bah, Quraysh clans disputed who held the honor of setting the Black Stone. Muhammad ﷺ spread a cloak, placed the stone upon it, and had every clan representative lift an edge together.
605-peletakan-hajar-aswad.facts:
Date : Around 605 CE (five years before prophethood)
Primary Location : The Ka'bah, Makkah
Arbitrator : Muhammad ﷺ (age 35)
Proposer of Arbitration : Abu Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi
Parties Involved : Major Quraysh clans (Banu Abd al-Dar, Banu Adi, Banu Hashim, Banu Makhzum)
605-peletakan-hajar-aswad.body:
Context & Background

Around 605 CE, when Muhammad ﷺ was thirty-five years old, heavy flash floods battered Makkah and weakened the walls of the Ka'bah, which then stood nine cubits high as dry-stacked stone without a roof. Structural deterioration had already exposed the sanctuary to theft and fire damage to its outer covering.

Quraysh leaders resolved to rebuild the sanctuary under a strict financial rule: only lawful earnings could fund the work, excluding usury, extortion, or illicit proceeds. Clans divided the perimeter walls among themselves and salvaged timber from a wrecked Byzantine merchant ship at the port of Shu'aybah to build the roof and columns.

Course of Events

1. Reconstruction and the Clan Dispute

Each clan laid stones smoothly until the walls reached the level of the Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad) at the southeastern corner. At that moment, fierce rivalry erupted over which clan deserved the honor of lifting the stone into its niche.

  • Key Point: The deadlock lasted four or five nights; Banu Abd al-Dar and Banu Adi ibn Ka'b even dipped their hands into a bowl of blood in a solemn pact to fight over the privilege.

2. Abu Umayyah's Proposal and Arrival of Al-Amin

Seeking to avert bloodshed in the sanctuary, the eldest Quraysh statesman, Abu Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, proposed letting the next person who entered through the gate of Banu Shaybah arbitrate the matter. Every clan consented to abide by the newcomer's ruling.

  • Key Point: The first person to walk through the gate was Muhammad ﷺ; recognizing him as Al-Amin, the assembled leaders immediately voiced their trust in his judgment.

3. The Shared Cloak Solution

After hearing the dispute, Muhammad ﷺ called for a cloak (rida'), spread it upon the ground, and placed the Black Stone in the center. He instructed a representative from each contending clan to grasp an edge of the fabric and raise the stone together to the height of the wall.

  • Key Point: Once lifted into position, he personally took the Black Stone and set it into the corner wall, ending the crisis without humiliating any clan.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The shared-cloak resolution prevented inter-clan warfare inside Makkah and solidified Muhammad's standing as a unifying arbiter five years before prophethood. Because lawful funds ran short before completion, Quraysh left roughly six to seven cubits on the northern side outside the roofed structure, enclosing it with the low semicircular wall known as Hijr Isma'il (al-Hatim).

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), al-Tabari's Tarikh (Shamela 23833), Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), and authenticated traditions on the Ka'bah's dimensions and Hijr Isma'il in Sunnah.com, alongside architectural context at ArchNet.

610-wahyu-pertama.title: The First Revelation
610-wahyu-pertama.summary: In 610 CE at the Cave of Hira, the angel Jibril delivered the first Quranic revelation—'Iqra' (Surah Al-Alaq 96:1-5)—initiating Muhammad's ﷺ prophetic mission.
610-wahyu-pertama.facts:
Date : 610 CE (Ramadan, at age 40)
Primary Location : Cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nur, Makkah
First Verses : Quran, Surah Al-Alaq (96:1-5)
Key Supporters : Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, Abu Bakr, Ali, Zayd ibn Harithah
Initial Phase : Quiet private preaching for roughly three years
610-wahyu-pertama.body:
Context & Background

As he approached forty years of age, Muhammad ﷺ regularly withdrew from Makkah's idolatrous rituals and social corruption for spiritual reflection (tahannuth) inside the Cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nur, roughly two miles from Makkah. During Ramadan, he took simple provisions and spent days in solitary contemplation before returning periodically to resupply.

For six months prior to the descent of the Quran, this period was preceded by true visions (al-ru'ya al-sadiqah) that unfolded with the clarity of dawn, as narrated by Aishah in Sahih al-Bukhari.

Course of Events

1. Arrival of Jibril and the Command 'Iqra'

On a night in Ramadan 610 CE, the angel Jibril appeared inside the Cave of Hira and commanded: "Read (Iqra')!" Muhammad ﷺ replied that he could not read. Jibril embraced him firmly, released him, and repeated the command three times before reciting the opening five verses of Surah Al-Alaq (96:1-5), proclaiming the Creator who formed humankind from a clinging clot and taught through the pen.

  • Key Point: From its opening lines, the revelation linked strict monotheism with learning and written knowledge.

2. Khadijah's Steadfastness and Waraqah ibn Nawfal

Trembling, the Prophet ﷺ hurried home to Khadijah and asked to be covered. Once calm, he recounted what transpired at Hira and voiced concern for himself. Khadijah reassured him by pointing to his lifelong conduct: maintaining family ties, bearing the burdens of the vulnerable, aiding the destitute, honoring guests, and standing by truth.

  • Key Point: Khadijah brought him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, a scholar of Hebrew scripture, who confirmed that the visitor was the same Namus (Jibril) sent to Moses and warned that his own tribe would eventually expel him.

3. Pause in Revelation and the Early Circle

Following a brief pause in revelation (fatrat al-wahy), the opening verses of Surah Al-Muddaththir (74:1-5) were revealed, instructing him to rise and warn. Over the next three years, preaching proceeded discreetly within close circles: Khadijah, Ali ibn Abi Thalib, Zayd ibn Harithah, and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who soon brought in Uthman ibn Affan, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abdurrahman ibn Awf, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

  • Key Point: Instruction in Quranic recitation and prayer centered privately at Dar al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam near Mount Safa.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The night at Hira marked the inception of the Quranic revelation and formed the core community of early believers (al-sabiqun al-awwalun) inside Makkah. Three years of quiet spiritual cultivation forged the resilience required to endure persecution, boycotts, and eventual migration.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative derives from Aishah's report in the Book of Revelation of Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim via Sunnah.com, Surah Al-Alaq and Surah Al-Muddaththir on Quran.com, Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), and Ar-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Archive.org). Physical appearances of the Prophet ﷺ, Khadijah, or Jibril are omitted in full observance of Islamic ethics.

613-dakwah-terang-terangan.title: Public Preaching Begins
613-dakwah-terang-terangan.summary: After roughly three years of quiet preaching, the Prophet ﷺ was commanded in 613 CE to proclaim Islam openly, triggering fierce opposition and persecution from Quraysh leaders.
613-dakwah-terang-terangan.facts:
Date : 613 CE (fourth year of prophethood)
Primary Location : Mount Safa and vicinity of the Ka'bah, Makkah
Quranic Basis : Surah Al-Shu'ara (26:214) & Surah Al-Hijr (15:94)
Key Opponents : Abu Lahab, Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt
Early Persecuted Believers : Yasir's family (Ammar, Yasir, Sumayyah), Bilal ibn Rabah, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt
613-dakwah-terang-terangan.body:
Context & Background

Following three years of discreet preaching in Makkah, the early Muslim community numbered dozens of believers drawn from aristocratic clans, freedmen, and vulnerable residents. This quiet period built internal solidarity before the message entered Makkah's public arena.

In 613 CE, two Quranic commands shifted the mission outward: Surah Al-Shu'ara (26:214) instructed the Prophet ﷺ to warn his closest kinsmen (Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muthalib), followed by Surah Al-Hijr (15:94), commanding open proclamation regardless of opposition.

Course of Events

1. Gatherings with Close Kinsmen

Acting on the first command, the Prophet ﷺ invited roughly forty-five members of Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muthalib to a meal. Before he could speak, his uncle Abu Lahab interrupted and dispersed the guests. At a second gathering, he delivered the call to monotheism plainly; Abu Thalib pledged continued tribal protection even while declining to abandon ancestral religion.

  • Key Point: The earliest vocal rejection came from within the Prophet's own extended family through Abu Lahab.

2. Proclamation on Mount Safa

The Prophet ﷺ then climbed Mount Safa beside the sanctuary and sounded the traditional Arab alarm cry to summon the clans of Quraysh. Once representatives of Banu Fihr, Banu Adi, and others gathered, he asked whether they would believe him if he warned of an enemy cavalry behind the hill. They answered unanimously in the affirmative, testifying to his lifelong truthfulness.

  • Key Point: When he called them to worship God alone and warned of judgment, Abu Lahab shouted curses against him, prompting the revelation of Surah Al-Masad (111).

3. Escalation of Persecution and Propaganda

Following the public proclamation, Quraysh chiefs led by Abu Jahl (Amr ibn Hisham), Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah organized coordinated suppression. They pressured Abu Thalib to silence his nephew while subjecting unprotected converts to public torture under the desert sun.

  • Key Point: Sumayyah bint Khayyat and her husband Yasir became the first martyrs of Islam under Abu Jahl's abuse, while Bilal ibn Rabah endured torture by Umayyah ibn Khalaf until ransomed by Abu Bakr.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Open preaching in 613 CE drew an unmistakable boundary between Quraysh oligarchic authority and the emerging monotheistic community. Despite organized counter-propaganda coordinated at Dar al-Nadwah during pilgrimage seasons, visiting tribes heard the Quran directly and carried word of the new faith beyond Makkah.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Accounts of the kinship banquet, the Mount Safa address, and Surah Al-Masad follow Ibn Abbas's narration in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim via Sunnah.com alongside Quranic citations on Quran.com. Biographical details on early martyrs come from Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), and Suwar min Hayatis Sahabah (Archive.org).

615-hijrah-ke-habasyah.title: Migration to Abyssinia
615-hijrah-ke-habasyah.summary: In 615 CE, groups of persecuted Muslims crossed the Red Sea to seek refuge in Abyssinia, where King Ashhamah al-Najashi granted them full protection and rejected Quraysh's extradition envoys.
615-hijrah-ke-habasyah.facts:
Date : 615 CE (Rajab, fifth year of prophethood)
Primary Location : Kingdom of Aksum (Abyssinia / modern Ethiopia), via Port of Shu'aybah
Leaders of Migration : Uthman ibn Affan (first wave) & Ja'far ibn Abi Thalib (second wave)
Protecting Ruler : King Ashhamah al-Najashi
Quraysh Envoys : Amr ibn al-As & Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah
615-hijrah-ke-habasyah.body:
Context & Background

By the fifth year of prophethood (615 CE), physical abuse and social harassment against Muslims in Makkah intensified severely. Even converts from influential clans faced confinement or pressure from their own relatives, while vulnerable followers endured daily public torment.

To preserve their faith and lives, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ advised believers to migrate across the Red Sea to Abyssinia (the Kingdom of Aksum), noting that its Christian ruler, King Ashhamah al-Najashi, governed justly and allowed no one to be wronged within his realm.

Course of Events

1. First Wave Through the Port of Shu'aybah

In Rajab 615 CE, an initial party of twelve men and four women slipped out of Makkah toward the Red Sea port of Shu'aybah, led by Uthman ibn Affan and his wife Ruqayyah bint Muhammad ﷺ alongside al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abdurrahman ibn Awf, and Uthman ibn Maz'un. Hiring merchant vessels for half a dinar each, they set sail safely moments before Quraysh pursuers arrived on the shore.

  • Key Point: Misled later by false rumors that Quraysh had reconciled with the Prophet, some emigrants returned to Makkah only to find persecution worse than before.

2. Second Wave Under Ja'far ibn Abi Thalib

A larger second migration soon followed, comprising roughly eighty-three men and eighteen or nineteen women led by Ja'far ibn Abi Thalib. Alarmed by this diplomatic setback, Quraysh dispatched two skilled negotiators, Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah, bearing prized leatherwork gifts to Aksumite generals and the royal court to demand the Muslims' extradition.

  • Key Point: Although courtiers urged compliance after receiving the gifts, al-Najashi refused to surrender refugees without first hearing their own testimony.

3. Royal Hearing and the Recitation of Surah Maryam

Summoned before al-Najashi and his bishops, Ja'far ibn Abi Thalib outlined life before Islam and the core message of the Prophet ﷺ: abandoning idols, speaking truth, honoring trusts, upholding kinship, and abstaining from bloodshed. When Amr ibn al-As sought to provoke the clergy by questioning Muslim belief regarding Jesus, Ja'far recited the opening passages of Surah Maryam (Chapter 19).

  • Key Point: Moved by the recitation concerning Mary and Jesus, al-Najashi declared that it issued from the same light as Moses and Jesus, returned the Quraysh gifts, and guaranteed permanent sanctuary.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The migration to Abyssinia marked Islam's first cross-continental refuge and established lasting goodwill between the early Muslim community and the Aksumite state. Many emigrants remained safely in Abyssinia until 7 AH (628 CE), rejoining the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah at the time of Khaybar.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Details on both migration waves, Ja'far's address, and al-Najashi's ruling come from Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), al-Tabari's Tarikh (Shamela 23833), Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288), and hadith collections on Sunnah.com, with Surah Maryam referenced via Quran.com.

619-pemboikotan-dan-tahun-duka-cita.title: Boycott & Year of Sorrow
619-pemboikotan-dan-tahun-duka-cita.summary: Following a three-year clan boycott in Shi'b Abi Thalib, both Abu Thalib and Khadijah passed away in 619 CE.

621-isra-dan-miraj.title: Isra' and Mi'raj
621-isra-dan-miraj.summary: Around 621 CE, the Prophet ﷺ was taken by night from Masjid al-Haram in Makkah to Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem and ascended through the heavens, receiving the obligation of five daily prayers.
621-isra-dan-miraj.facts:
Date : Around 621 CE (prior to the Hijrah to Madinah)
Route : Masjid al-Haram (Makkah) -> Masjid al-Aqsa (Jerusalem) -> Sidrat al-Muntaha
Core Obligation : Five daily prayers
Principal Supporter : Abu Bakr al-Siddiq
Quranic References : Surah Al-Isra' (17:1) & Surah Al-Najm (53:13-18)
621-isra-dan-miraj.body:
Context & Background

The period between the tenth and twelfth years of prophethood marked the severest trial of the Makkan phase. Shortly after a three-year economic boycott in Shi'b Abi Thalib ended, the Year of Sorrow ('Am al-Huzn) brought the deaths of two key pillars of support: the Prophet's uncle and protector Abu Thalib and his wife Khadijah bint Khuwaylid.

Seeking new allies in nearby Ta'if alongside Zayd ibn Harithah, the Prophet ﷺ met harsh rejection and physical assault. Following his return to Makkah under the protection of al-Mut'im ibn Adi, the miraculous night journey and ascension (al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj) took place around 621 CE.

Course of Events

1. Night Journey to Masjid al-Aqsa (Isra')

From the precincts of Masjid al-Haram in Makkah, Jibril escorted the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by night on al-Buraq to Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem, Palestine, as commemorated in the opening verse of Surah Al-Isra' (17:1). At the sacred compound in Jerusalem, he led earlier prophets in congregational prayer, affirming the continuity of monotheistic revelation.

  • Key Point: Anchoring the Isra' in Masjid al-Aqsa directly tied Jerusalem to the spiritual heritage of the Muslim community while still in Makkah.

2. Ascension and the Five Daily Prayers (Mi'raj)

From Jerusalem, the Prophet ﷺ ascended with Jibril through the seven heavens up to Sidrat al-Muntaha (Surah Al-Najm 53:13-18), encountering earlier prophets across each realm including Adam, Yahya, Isa, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa, and Ibrahim. At the summit, daily prayer was prescribed directly: originally fifty prayers per day, reduced upon repeated petitions advised by Moses to five daily prayers carrying the reward of fifty.

  • Key Point: Unlike other obligations revealed on earth, the five daily prayers were instituted directly during the Mi'raj.

3. Testing in Makkah and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq

The next morning near the Ka'bah, Quraysh chiefs mocked his account of traveling to Jerusalem and back in a single night, as caravans normally required a month for the round trip. Traders familiar with Syria demanded architectural details of Masjid al-Aqsa and news of approaching caravans; he accurately described both the sanctuary's features and an inbound caravan. Meanwhile, Abu Bakr affirmed the event without hesitation, earning lasting recognition as al-Siddiq (the Truthful).

  • Key Point: When the caravan arrived days later, it confirmed every detail and sequence the Prophet ﷺ had reported.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Isra' and Mi'raj established the five daily prayers as the daily anchor of Muslim life and tested the conviction of Makkan believers on the eve of the Hijrah to Madinah. It also underscored Jerusalem's status as Islam's first direction of prayer (qiblah) and one of its three sacred mosques.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This entry is grounded in Surah Al-Isra' (17:1) and Surah Al-Najm (53:13-18) via Quran.com, authenticated narrations in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim via Sunnah.com, Ibn Hisham's As-Sirah an-Nabawiyyah (Shamela 9783), and Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela 12288). Historians record multiple opinions on the exact month (c. 620-621 CE, commonly observed on 27 Rajab alongside reports citing Rabi' al-Awwal or Rabi' al-Akhir). No physical depiction of any prophet is included.

622-hijrah-ke-madinah.title: Hijrah to Medina
622-hijrah-ke-madinah.summary: Following the Pledges of Aqabah, the Prophet ﷺ migrated with Abu Bakr from Mecca to Yathrib, later known as Medina, marking the start of the Islamic Hijri calendar.
622-hijrah-ke-madinah.body:
Context & Historical Background

In 622 CE, after thirteen years of preaching in Mecca, persecution against Muslims intensified following the deaths of Abu Talib and Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. Several companions had already sought refuge in Abyssinia, while residents of Yathrib pledged protection during the First Pledge of Aqabah (621 CE) with twelve delegates and the Second Pledge of Aqabah (622 CE) with seventy-three men and two women from the Aws and Khazraj tribes.

Alarmed by the rise of a safe haven to the north, Quraysh leaders convened at Dar al-Nadwah. Following Abu Jahl's proposal, they selected one armed youth from each clan to besiege the house of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at night so that responsibility for the killing would be dispersed across all Meccan tribes.

Course of Events

1. The Night Siege and Refuge in Cave Thawr

  • Key Point: On the night of 27 Safar, 1 AH, Ali ibn Abi Talib slept in the Prophet's bed to distract the besiegers and later return entrusted deposits to Meccan owners. The Prophet ﷺ departed with Abu Bakr al-Siddiq southward toward Mount Thawr rather than north toward Yathrib.

They remained inside Cave Thawr for three nights. Abu Bakr's son Abdullah monitored Quraysh search parties in Mecca and delivered updates each night, while Asma bint Abi Bakr brought food supplies. Amir ibn Fuhayrah grazed sheep near the cave before dawn to erase footprints and provide milk.

2. The Coastal Route and Suraqah ibn Malik

  • Key Point: Quraysh offered a bounty of one hundred camels for capturing the travelers. Guided by Abdullah ibn Urayqit of Banu al-Dil, the party took an unfamiliar coastal route along the Red Sea in early Rabi al-Awwal.

Suraqah ibn Malik tracked them on horseback in pursuit of the reward. Each time he closed in, his horse's hooves sank into the sand, prompting him to halt the chase, request a written pledge of safety, and turn back to misdirect other Meccan scouts.

3. Arrival in Quba and Entry into Yathrib

  • Key Point: The party reached Quba on the southern outskirts of Yathrib in Rabi al-Awwal 1 AH (September 622 CE) and established the Quba Mosque, the first mosque built in Islam.

After staying briefly with Kulthum ibn al-Hidm, they proceeded toward central Yathrib on Friday, stopping in the Valley of Ranuna among Banu Salim ibn Awf for the first Friday congregational prayer. Inside Yathrib, the Prophet's camel knelt on land owned by two orphans, Sahl and Suhayl of Banu Najjar, which was purchased to construct Al-Masjid al-Nabawi while the Prophet ﷺ stayed as a guest of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.

Impact & Historical Legacy

Yathrib became known as Madinat al-Nabi (Medina) and evolved into the first Islamic polity. The Prophet ﷺ instituted a pact of brotherhood pairing Meccan emigrants (Muhajirun) with Medinan hosts (Ansar) and drafted the Constitution of Medina (Sahifat al-Madinah) defining mutual defense and legal rights among Muslim and Jewish tribes.

During the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab in 17 AH, the year of the Hijrah (622 CE) was formally designated as Year 1 of the Hijri lunar calendar.

Methodology Notes (About This Telling)

This narrative draws directly from Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham, Tarikh al-Tabari, and Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh by Ibn al-Athir, corroborated with authenticated reports in Sunnah.com and Quranic reference to Surah al-Tawbah (9:40) on Quran.com. In accordance with Islamic representational standards, no physical depiction of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is included.
622-hijrah-ke-madinah.facts:
Year : 622 CE / 1 AH
Location : Mecca, Cave Thawr, Quba, Yathrib (Medina)
Key Figures : Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abdullah ibn Urayqit
Route : Western Red Sea coastal trail
Outcome : Establishment of Medina as an Islamic polity and start of the Hijri calendar

624-perang-badar.title: Battle of Badr
624-perang-badar.summary: The first major military confrontation between an outnumbered Muslim force from Medina and a larger Quraysh army, ending in Muslim victory and the death of Abu Jahl.
624-perang-badar.body:
Context & Historical Background

After the migration to Medina in 622 CE, Quraysh leaders in Mecca confiscated the homes and property left behind by the Muhajirun. To counter Meccan hostility and recover lost wealth, Medina monitored Quraysh trade caravans traveling between Mecca and Syria. In Ramadan 2 AH (March 624 CE), intelligence reached Medina that Abu Sufyan ibn Harb was returning from Syria with a massive caravan of roughly one thousand camels carrying goods valued at fifty thousand dinars.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ led a lightly armed force of about 313 to 317 men—with only two horses and seventy camels shared in rotation—to intercept the caravan. Alerted in advance, Abu Sufyan dispatched Damdam ibn Amr al-Ghifari to summon military reinforcements from Mecca and diverted his caravan safely along the Red Sea coast.

Course of Events

1. Quraysh Mobilization and Control of the Wells

  • Key Point: Although Abu Sufyan sent word that the caravan was safe, Abu Jahl (Amr ibn Hisham) insisted on marching nearly one thousand fighters, including one hundred cavalrymen and seven hundred camels, to the Valley of Badr to crush Medina.

Facing an armed army instead of a trade escort, the Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions. Abu Bakr, Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Miqdad ibn Amr for the Muhajirun, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh for the Ansar affirmed full support. Upon reaching Badr, roughly 130 kilometers southwest of Medina, al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir advised occupying the well closest to the enemy and filling in the rear wells to deny Quraysh access to water.

2. Opening Duels and Engagement

  • Key Point: On the morning of Friday, 17 Ramadan 2 AH (13 March 624 CE), overnight rain compacted the sand beneath the Muslim lines while turning the Quraysh side of the valley muddy.

Before general combat began, three Quraysh notables—Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn Utbah—issued a challenge for single combat. Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ubaydah ibn al-Harith stepped forward; Hamzah and Ali swiftly slew their opponents and assisted Ubaydah, who later died of his leg wound at al-Safra.

3. Collapse of the Meccan Lines

  • Key Point: Fighting in disciplined ranks rather than loose tribal charges, the Muslim force absorbed the initial Quraysh assault before counterattacking decisively.

Two young Ansar fighters, Mu'adh ibn Amr ibn al-Jamuh and Mu'awwidh ibn Afra, broke through the Meccan guard and fatally wounded Abu Jahl, whose death was completed by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. Seventy Quraysh fighters were killed—including senior leaders Umayyah ibn Khalaf and Utbah ibn Rabi'ah—and seventy were captured, while fourteen Muslims fell as martyrs (six Muhajirun and eight Ansar).

Impact & Historical Legacy

Victory at Badr transformed Medina into an established political and military force across the Hijaz. Conversely, the loss of veteran Meccan leadership shattered Quraysh prestige and fueled the revenge campaign led by Abu Sufyan at Uhud the following year.

Captives from Badr were treated humanely: wealthier prisoners paid ransom for release, while literate captives earned freedom by teaching ten Medinan children how to read and write.

Methodology Notes (About This Telling)

This account follows Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham, Tarikh al-Tabari, and Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh by Ibn al-Athir, cross-referenced with Surah al-Anfal on Quran.com and authenticated narrations on Sunnah.com. Figures and dates reflect consensus ranges across primary Arabic chronicles.
624-perang-badar.facts:
Date : 17 Ramadan 2 AH / March 624 CE
Location : Valley of Badr, southwest of Medina
Forces : Approx. 313 Muslims vs. 1,000 Quraysh fighters
Key Figures : Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir, Abu Jahl
Casualties : 14 Muslims martyred; 70 Quraysh killed and 70 captured

625-perang-uhud.title: Battle of Uhud
625-perang-uhud.summary: Fought at the foot of Mount Uhud north of Medina. Muslim archers left their assigned hill, allowing Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry to strike from the rear; Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib was martyred.
625-perang-uhud.body:
Context & Historical Background

Following the defeat at Badr, Quraysh leaders dedicated the entire profit of Abu Sufyan's saved caravan to finance a retaliatory campaign against Medina. In Shawwal 3 AH (March 625 CE), Abu Sufyan ibn Harb marched north with roughly 3,000 warriors, 200 cavalrymen, 700 armored troops, and 3,000 camels, encamping near Mount Uhud roughly five kilometers north of Medina.

Inside Medina, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ favored defending from within the city, a view shared by Abdullah ibn Ubayy, whereas younger companions eager to fight outside the city carried the majority. Around 1,000 Muslim troops marched out, but Abdullah ibn Ubayy defected midway at al-Shawt with 300 followers, leaving roughly 700 Muslim infantry facing a much larger army.

Course of Events

1. Deployment and the Archers on Mount Aynayn

  • Key Point: Positioning Mount Uhud at his back, the Prophet ﷺ stationed fifty archers under Abdullah ibn Jubayr atop Mount Aynayn (Archers' Hill) on the left flank.

He issued strict orders prohibiting the archers from leaving their elevated post under any circumstance—whether victorious or hard-pressed—to prevent Meccan cavalry from circling behind the Muslim lines.

2. Early Muslim Advantage and Breach of Discipline

  • Key Point: At the outset, Muslim champions struck down successive Quraysh standard-bearers from Banu Abd al-Dar, while Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Dujanah drove the Meccan infantry back toward their camp.

Seeing the Quraysh lines retreat, roughly forty of the fifty archers descended Mount Aynayn to gather spoils despite Abdullah ibn Jubayr's repeated warnings, leaving fewer than ten defenders on the ridge.

3. Khalid ibn al-Walid's Flanking Charge

  • Key Point: Spotting the exposed flank, Khalid ibn al-Walid—then commanding Quraysh's right cavalry wing—swept behind Mount Aynayn, overwhelmed Abdullah ibn Jubayr's remaining archers, and charged into the Muslim rear.

Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl rallied the Meccan front, trapping the Muslim force in a pincer movement. Wahshi ibn Harb fatally struck Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib with a javelin, and standard-bearer Mus'ab ibn Umayr fell amidst false rumors of the Prophet's death. A steadfast group including Abu Dujanah, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Talhah ibn Ubaydillah, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Nusaybah bint Ka'b shielded the wounded Prophet ﷺ as the survivors withdrew up the rocky slopes of Uhud.

Impact & Historical Legacy

Approximately seventy Muslims were martyred at Uhud, mostly from the Ansar, compared to twenty-two to thirty-seven Quraysh dead. Too exhausted to assault Medina itself, Abu Sufyan's army withdrew toward Mecca.

The next morning, the Prophet ﷺ led wounded survivors as far as Hamra al-Asad, eight miles south of Medina, to demonstrate unbroken resolve. Surah Ali Imran (3:121–179) records the lessons of Uhud regarding obedience to military command and the danger of premature pursuit of spoils.

Methodology Notes (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham, Tarikh al-Tabari, and biographical notices in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala by al-Dhahabi, alongside Surah Ali Imran on Quran.com and hadith collections on Sunnah.com. In accordance with Islamic representational ethics, no physical description of the Prophet ﷺ is included.
625-perang-uhud.facts:
Date : Shawwal 3 AH / March 625 CE
Location : Foot and slopes of Mount Uhud, north of Medina
Forces : Approx. 700 Muslims vs. 3,000 Quraysh troops
Key Figures : Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Abdullah ibn Jubayr, Khalid ibn al-Walid, Abu Sufyan
Casualties : Approx. 70 Muslims martyred; 22-37 Quraysh killed

627-perang-khandaq.title: Battle of the Trench (Khandaq)
627-perang-khandaq.summary: A 10,000-strong confederate coalition besieged Medina. On the advice of Salman al-Farisi, Muslims dug a defensive trench across the northern approach and successfully defended the city.
627-perang-khandaq.body:
Context & Historical Background

In 5 AH (627 CE), exiled leaders of Banu Nadir such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq lobbied Mecca and tribes across Najd to assemble an unprecedented coalition against Medina. Quraysh joined forces with Ghatafan, Banu Sulaym, Banu Asad, Banu Murrah, and Fazarah, forming the Confederates (al-Ahzab) numbering roughly 10,000 fighters under the overall command of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

Medina could muster around 3,000 defenders. Facing an overwhelming numerical disparity in Shawwal 5 AH (March–April 627 CE), engaging the coalition in an open desert battle risked total defeat, requiring an innovative defensive plan.

Course of Events

1. Salman al-Farisi's Trench Across the Northern Gap

  • Key Point: During the war council, Salman al-Farisi proposed excavating a wide defensive trench (khandaq), a Persian siege-defense method previously unknown in Arabian warfare.

Medina's eastern, western, and southern flanks were naturally shielded by jagged volcanic lava fields (Harrat Waqim and Harrat al-Wabarah) and dense date-palm groves. Only the northern plain lay open, so the defenders dug an approximately 5.5-kilometer trench stretching from Shaykhayn to Mount Dhubab and al-Madhad despite winter cold and severe food shortages.

2. The Siege and Banu Qurayzah's Defection

  • Key Point: Halted abruptly by the trench, the 10,000 coalition troops settled into a month-long standoff marked mainly by archery exchanges across the ditch.

Only a few horsemen managed to leap across a narrow section, including the Quraysh champion Amr ibn Abd Wudd, who was slain in single combat by Ali ibn Abi Talib. The siege grew perilous when Huyayy ibn Akhtab persuaded Ka'b ibn Asad, leader of Banu Qurayzah in southern Medina, to annul their defense pact with Medina and threaten the city from the rear.

3. Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud's Diplomacy and the Storm

  • Key Point: Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud of Ghatafan, who had secretly embraced Islam, executed a diplomatic ruse that sowed deep mutual distrust among Banu Qurayzah, Quraysh, and Ghatafan.

He advised Banu Qurayzah to demand Quraysh hostages before joining combat, while warning Quraysh that Banu Qurayzah planned to hand those hostages over to Medina. With coalition unity fractured, an intense, freezing night storm tore down tents, scattered campfires, and overturned cooking pots, prompting Abu Sufyan to order a full withdrawal.

Impact & Historical Legacy

With only six Muslim martyrs and minimal coalition fatalities, the failed siege marked a decisive turning point. Immediately afterward, Medina addressed Banu Qurayzah's treaty breach under the arbitration of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, whom the tribe accepted as judge.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ declared that Quraysh would never again mount an offensive against Medina, signaling that strategic initiative had permanently shifted to the Muslims, as commemorated in Surah al-Ahzab.

Methodology Notes (About This Telling)

This narrative synthesizes Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham, Tarikh al-Tabari, and Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh by Ibn al-Athir, corroborated by Surah al-Ahzab on Quran.com and hadith reports on Sunnah.com. In accordance with Islamic representational standards, no physical depiction of the Prophet ﷺ is included.
627-perang-khandaq.facts:
Date : Shawwal-Dhu al-Qa'dah 5 AH / 627 CE
Location : Northern approach of Medina between Harrat Waqim and Harrat al-Wabarah
Forces : Approx. 3,000 Muslims vs. 10,000 Confederates
Key Figures : Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Salman al-Farisi, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sufyan
Outcome : Siege failed; the Confederate coalition withdrew without entering Medina

628-perjanjian-hudaibiyah.title: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
628-perjanjian-hudaibiyah.summary: The Prophet ﷺ and Muslims set out for Mecca to perform umrah, were halted by Quraysh, and concluded a truce that opened the path for peaceful expansion of Islam.
628-perjanjian-hudaibiyah.body:
Context & Historical Background

Following Quraysh's failure to overrun Medina at the Battle of the Trench in 627 CE, Meccan offensive strength declined. In Dhu al-Qa'dah 6 AH (March 628 CE)—one of the four sacred months during which Arab custom forbade warfare—the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saw a vision of Muslims entering the Sacred Mosque safely and called for an unarmed umrah pilgrimage to Mecca.

Roughly 1,400 to 1,500 companions departed Medina wearing ihram garments, carrying only sheathed travelers' swords, and leading about seventy sacrificial camels to signal peaceful intent.

Course of Events

1. Quraysh Blockade and the Pledge of Ridwan

  • Key Point: Refusing entry into Mecca, Quraysh dispatched two hundred horsemen under Khalid ibn al-Walid and Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl to Kura al-Ghamim to block the main approach.

To avoid bloodshed, the Prophet ﷺ guided the pilgrims along rugged mountain trails to Hudaybiyyah, roughly twenty-two kilometers southwest of Mecca. Envoys including Budayl ibn Warqa and Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi shuttled between the camps before the Prophet ﷺ sent Uthman ibn Affan into Mecca due to his Umayyad kinship. When Uthman's return was delayed and rumors spread of his murder, the Prophet ﷺ took a solemn oath of steadfastness from his companions beneath a tree, known as Bay'at al-Ridwan.

2. Negotiations with Suhayl ibn Amr

  • Key Point: Alarmed by the unity displayed in Bay'at al-Ridwan, Quraysh released Uthman and sent Suhayl ibn Amr to negotiate a formal settlement.

Ali ibn Abi Talib served as scribe. Suhayl objected to writing "Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim" and the title "Messenger of God," insisting instead on "Bismikallahumma" and "Muhammad ibn Abdullah," concessions the Prophet ﷺ accepted to secure peace.

3. Terms of the Treaty

  • Key Point: Both parties agreed to a ten-year truce; deferral of umrah until the next year for a three-day stay with sheathed swords; extradition of Meccan converts fleeing to Medina without guardian permission (while Medinans defecting to Mecca would not be returned); and freedom for Arab tribes to ally with either side.

Immediately afterward, Banu Khuza'ah entered a pact with Medina while Banu Bakr aligned with Quraysh. Though Umar ibn al-Khattab and others initially questioned the extradition clause, the Prophet ﷺ upheld the signed agreement.

Impact & Historical Legacy

On the return journey, Surah al-Fath was revealed describing Hudaybiyyah as a "clear victory" (Fathan Mubina). For the first time, Quraysh formally recognized Medina as an equal sovereign party to an interstate treaty.

During the ensuing truce, the Prophet ﷺ sent diplomatic envoys with letters to rulers including Heraclius of Byzantium, Khosrow of Persia, al-Muqawqis of Egypt, and the Negus of Abyssinia. Within two years, the Muslim community grew dramatically, expanding from 1,400 pilgrims at Hudaybiyyah to 10,000 troops entering Mecca in 630 CE.

Methodology Notes (About This Telling)

This narrative draws upon Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham, Tarikh al-Tabari, and Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh by Ibn al-Athir, alongside the detailed report of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah on Sunnah.com and Surah al-Fath on Quran.com. No physical description of the Prophet ﷺ appears in accordance with Islamic ethical rules.
628-perjanjian-hudaibiyah.facts:
Date : Dhu al-Qa'dah 6 AH / March 628 CE
Location : Hudaybiyyah, approx. 22 km southwest of Mecca
Delegates : Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Uthman ibn Affan, Ali ibn Abi Talib; Suhayl ibn Amr (Quraysh)
Key Terms : 10-year truce, umrah deferred to 7 AH, open tribal alliances
Outcome : Formal political recognition of Medina and peaceful expansion of Islam

630-fathu-makkah.title: Conquest of Mecca (Fath Makkah)
630-fathu-makkah.summary: The Prophet ﷺ entered Mecca with a 10,000-strong army nearly without bloodshed, granted general amnesty to the Meccans, and cleared the idols surrounding the Kaaba.
630-fathu-makkah.body:
Context & Historical Background

The ten-year Treaty of Hudaybiyyah collapsed in its second year when Banu Bakr, allied with Quraysh, launched a surprise night raid in Sha'ban 8 AH (629 CE) against Banu Khuza'ah—allies of Medina—at the wells of al-Watir, killing over twenty people even inside the sacred sanctuary. Several Quraysh leaders including Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Safwan ibn Umayyah, and Suhayl ibn Amr secretly supplied weapons and personnel for the attack.

After Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i appealed to Medina for protection, Abu Sufyan traveled to Medina hoping to renew the truce, but his mission failed. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ ordered confidential mobilization, sealing roads toward Mecca until 10,000 troops gathered from the Muhajirun, Ansar, and allied tribes including Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ashja, Sulaym, and Ghifar.

Course of Events

1. Silent March to Marr al-Zahran

  • Key Point: Departing on 10 Ramadan 8 AH, the army encamped at Marr al-Zahran and lit 10,000 campfires across the valley at night to demonstrate overwhelming strength and deter armed resistance.

Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib brought Abu Sufyan—who had ridden out to scout—into the Muslim camp, where Abu Sufyan embraced Islam. The Prophet ﷺ granted immunity to anyone who entered Abu Sufyan's house, remained behind locked doors, or took shelter inside the Sacred Mosque.

2. Four-Column Entry into Mecca

  • Key Point: On 20 Ramadan 8 AH (January 630 CE), the 10,000-strong army entered Mecca simultaneously along four routes under strict orders not to fight unless attacked.

Khalid ibn al-Walid advanced from the lower southern entrance, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam entered from the northern heights of Kada, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah led infantry through the central valley, and the Ansar contingent approached from the west. Three columns met no resistance; only Khalid ibn al-Walid's sector faced an armed ambush by Ikrimah and Safwan at Khandamah, resulting in roughly twelve to twenty-eight Quraysh fatalities and two Muslim martyrs.

3. Cleansing the Kaaba and General Amnesty

  • Key Point: Circling the Kaaba seven times, the Prophet ﷺ ordered the removal and destruction of roughly 360 idols around the sanctuary while reciting Surah al-Isra (17:81).

After praying inside the Kaaba and instructing Bilal ibn Rabah to sound the call to prayer from its roof, he addressed the assembled Meccans in the courtyard and proclaimed a general amnesty: "Go, for you are free."

Impact & Historical Legacy

The nearly bloodless conquest of Mecca ended decades of Quraysh hostility against Islam, while the keys of the Kaaba were entrusted back to Uthman ibn Talhah of Banu Shaybah as a hereditary custodianship.

Following Mecca's capitulation, delegations from tribes across the Arabian Peninsula streamed into Medina throughout 9 AH, earning that year the title Year of Delegations (Am al-Wufud).

Methodology Notes (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham, Tarikh al-Tabari, and Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh by Ibn al-Athir, corroborated by authenticated reports in Sunnah.com and Surah al-Isra (17:81) on Quran.com. No physical depiction of the Prophet ﷺ is included in accordance with Islamic representational standards.
630-fathu-makkah.facts:
Date : 20 Ramadan 8 AH / January 630 CE
Location : Mecca
Forces : 10,000 Muslim troops in 4 columns
Key Figures : Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Khalid ibn al-Walid, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Abu Sufyan, Bilal ibn Rabah
Outcome : Peaceful takeover of Mecca, cleansing of the Kaaba, and general amnesty

632-haji-wada-dan-wafatnya-nabi.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage and the Passing of the Prophet
632-haji-wada-dan-wafatnya-nabi.summary: The Prophet ﷺ performed his final pilgrimage and delivered the Farewell Sermon at Arafah, passing away shortly thereafter in Madinah on 12 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH.
632-haji-wada-dan-wafatnya-nabi.body:
Context & Background

By late 10 AH, the Arabian Peninsula stood united under Islamic governance following the Conquest of Makkah, the Battle of Hunayn, and the Tabuk expedition. Tribal delegations arrived steadily in Madinah to pledge allegiance in what historians call the Year of Delegations. On 25 Dhu al-Qa'dah 10 AH (February 632 CE), Prophet Muhammad ﷺ announced his intention to perform Hajj. Over one hundred thousand Muslims converged on Madinah and marched toward Makkah for what became the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada'), the first and final Hajj led directly by the Prophet ﷺ.

Course of Events

1. Departure and Ihram at Dhu al-Hulayfah

  • Key Point: The caravan departed Madinah on Saturday, 25 Dhu al-Qa'dah 10 AH, entered the state of ihram at Dhu al-Hulayfah, and reached Makkah on 4 Dhu al-Hijjah after a nine-day journey.

  • Key Point: Upon completing circumambulation of the Ka'bah and walking between Safa and Marwah, the Prophet ﷺ proceeded to Mina on 8 Dhu al-Hijjah (Day of Tarwiyah).

2. The Farewell Sermon at Arafah

  • Key Point: On Friday, 9 Dhu al-Hijjah 10 AH (6 March 632 CE), in the Uranah valley at Arafah, the Prophet ﷺ addressed the assembled pilgrims.

  • Key Point: The sermon declared the inviolability of life, property, and honor, abolished pre-Islamic usury beginning with the claims of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, annulled tribal blood feuds, affirmed mutual marital rights, and urged steadfast adherence to the Qur'an.

  • Key Point: At Arafah, Surah al-Ma'idah verse 3 was revealed, proclaiming the completion of the religion before pilgrims continued to Muzdalifah and Mina.

3. Usamah's Expedition and Final Illness

  • Key Point: After returning to Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ ordered an expedition toward Balqa' on the Syrian frontier under Usamah ibn Zayd in late Safar 11 AH.

  • Key Point: Stricken with a severe fever, he obtained consent from his wives to be nursed in the chamber of Aisyah radhiyallahu 'anha and designated Abu Bakr al-Siddiq to lead congregational prayers at al-Masjid al-Nabawi.

4. Passing on 12 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH

  • Key Point: On Monday morning, 12 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH (8 June 632 CE), after lifting the curtain to observe the congregation praying behind Abu Bakr, the Prophet ﷺ passed away before noon at the age of sixty-three.

  • Key Point: Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Abbas, al-Fadl, Qutham, Usamah ibn Zayd, and Shuqran prepared the body and buried him inside Aisyah's chamber on Tuesday night.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The Prophet's passing ended the era of Qur'anic revelation and confronted Madinah with an immediate succession crisis. Umar ibn al-Khattab initially refused to accept the news until Abu Bakr recited Surah Ali Imran verse 144 to steady the community. That same afternoon, Ansar and Muhajirun leaders convened at Saqifah Bani Sa'idah, establishing the caliphate with Abu Bakr as the first caliph. The Farewell Sermon remained a foundational charter in Islamic jurisprudence on human sanctity, abolition of tribal supremacy, and civic accountability on the eve of expansion into Syria, Iraq, and Egypt.

Methodological Note (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on classical primary sources and strictly avoids any physical or visual depiction of the Prophet ﷺ or the Mothers of the Believers in accordance with Islamic scholarly etiquette. Cross-references include Quran.com, Sunnah.com, Ibn Hisham's al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, Tarikh al-Tabari, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, and Ar-Rahiq al-Makhtum.
632-haji-wada-dan-wafatnya-nabi.facts:
Year : 10–11 AH / 632 CE
Location : Dhu al-Hulayfah, Arafah, Mina, and Madinah
Key Figures : Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Usamah ibn Zayd
Primary Sources : Qur'an (5:3), Sirah Ibn Hisham, Tarikh al-Tabari, Al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah

632-abu-bakar-menjadi-khalifah.title: Abu Bakr Becomes Caliph
632-abu-bakar-menjadi-khalifah.summary: Abu Bakr was pledged allegiance as the first caliph and quelled widespread apostasy and false prophets in the Riddah Wars, notably defeating Musaylimah at Yamamah.
632-abu-bakar-menjadi-khalifah.body:
Context & Background

The passing of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ on 12 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH (8 June 632 CE) left Madinah without a prophetic successor or a written procedure for headship of state. Immediately, several Arabian tribes treated their political allegiance and zakat obligations as personal pacts that expired with the Prophet's death. Rebels withheld zakat while rival claimants to prophethood—including Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab in Yamamah, Tulayhah ibn Khuwaylid in Najd, al-Aswad al-Ansi in Yemen, and Sajah among Banu Tamim—mobilized armed followings.

Course of Events

1. Saqifah Bani Sa'idah and the First Bay'ah

  • Key Point: On the day of the Prophet's passing, Ansar leaders gathered at Saqifah Bani Sa'idah alongside Sa'd ibn Ubadah before Abu Bakr, Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah joined the deliberation.

  • Key Point: Recognizing the Ansar's vital sacrifices while arguing that Arabian tribes would unite only under Quraysh leadership, Umar pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr, followed by a general public pledge at al-Masjid al-Nabawi on 13 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH.

  • Key Point: Despite threats surrounding Madinah, Abu Bakr insisted on dispatching Usamah ibn Zayd's expedition to Syria as ordered by the Prophet ﷺ.

2. The Riddah Wars and Battle of Yamamah (632–633 CE)

  • Key Point: Organizing eleven military brigades at Dhu al-Qassah, Abu Bakr sent commanders across Arabia; Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated Tulayhah at Buzakhah and pacified Najd.
