859-al-qarawiyyin-didirikan-di-fez.title: Founding of Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez
859-al-qarawiyyin-didirikan-di-fez.summary: Fatima al-Fihri founded the Al-Qarawiyyin mosque and center of learning in Fez in 859 CE, widely recognized as the oldest continuously operating university.
859-al-qarawiyyin-didirikan-di-fez.facts:
Date : 859 CE (245 AH)
Location : Fez, Morocco
Key Figures : Fatima al-Fihri, Yahya ibn Muhammad al-Idrisi
Outcome : Creation of Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque and enduring educational institution
Primary Sources : Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, ArchNet
859-al-qarawiyyin-didirikan-di-fez.body:
Context & Background

During the early ninth century, the Idrisid city of Fez in Morocco grew into a flourishing refuge for settlers from two major regions: migrants from Al-Andalus on the eastern bank of the Fez River and families from Kairouan in Tunisia on the western bank (Udwa al-Qarawiyyin).

Among the Kairouanese newcomers was a prosperous merchant, Muhammad ibn Abdallah al-Fihri, and his daughters Fatima and Maryam. Upon inheriting her family's wealth after the deaths of her father, brother, and husband, Fatima al-Fihri dedicated her fortune to constructing a spacious congregational mosque and place of study for the expanding western quarter.

Course of Events

1. Construction of Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque (859 CE)

  • Key Point: At the start of Ramadan 245 AH (859 CE), Fatima al-Fihri broke ground on Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque using materials quarried directly on site.

With authorization from Idrisid ruler Yahya ibn Muhammad, builders excavated local stone, water, and clay inside the grounds so the endowment stayed clear of disputed property. Moroccan historical tradition records that Fatima fasted throughout the initial construction, while her sister Maryam funded the Andalusian Mosque across the river.

2. Early Study Circles and Monumental Expansions

  • Key Point: From its inception, Al-Qarawiyyin hosted teaching circles in Qur'anic sciences, Maliki law, Arabic grammar, and foundational sciences.

Growing student enrollment prompted successive expansions: Zenata rulers added a square stone minaret in 956 CE, and the Almoravids enlarged the prayer hall extensively during the twelfth century with richly carved cupolas and muqarnas vaults.

3. A Cross-Mediterranean Hub of Learning

  • Key Point: Supported by endowed libraries and residential madrasas built during the Marinid period, Fez drew scholars from Iberia, North Africa, and the East.

Prominent figures linked to Al-Qarawiyyin's scholarly circles include geographer al-Idrisi, philosopher Ibn Bajjah, historian Ibn Khaldun, and Cordoban Jewish philosopher Maimonides.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Operating continuously for more than eleven centuries, Al-Qarawiyyin anchored Islamic scholarship in the Maghrib and bridged intellectual exchange between Al-Andalus and the Middle East. Today, UNESCO and Guinness World Records recognize it as the oldest continually operating degree-granting institution, and its historic library preserves thousands of medieval manuscripts.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Regional Idrisid history in the third century AH draws on Ibn al-Athir's Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and North African biographical notes in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, alongside architectural and historical records of Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque curated by ArchNet.

909-dinasti-fatimiyah-berdiri.title: Rise of the Fatimid Dynasty
909-dinasti-fatimiyah-berdiri.summary: The Fatimid Caliphate established power in Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia) in 909 CE before later expanding eastward into Egypt.
909-dinasti-fatimiyah-berdiri.facts:
Date : 909–910 CE (296–297 AH)
Location : Raqqada and Kairouan, Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia)
Key Figures : Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi Billah, Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, Ziyadat Allah III
Outcome : Overthrow of the Aghlabids and creation of the Fatimid Caliphate
Primary Sources : Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, Tarikh al-Tabari, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala
909-dinasti-fatimiyah-berdiri.body:
Context & Background

By the late ninth century, Abbasid authority in Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia and eastern Algeria) had steadily eroded. The autonomous Aghlabid dynasty in Kairouan suffered from dynastic bloodshed, heavy taxation, and popular discontent under Amir Ziyadat Allah III.

Exploiting this vacuum, the Ismaili missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i arrived in the mountains of Lesser Kabylia in 893 CE and forged a disciplined politico-military following among the Kutama Berber confederation.

Course of Events

1. Collapse of Aghlabid Rule at Raqqada (March 909 CE)

  • Key Point: Kutama Berber forces led by Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i defeated the Aghlabid army and seized the royal city of Raqqada near Kairouan.

Following a decisive Aghlabid defeat at al-Aribus, Ziyadat Allah III fled east toward Egypt with the state treasury. Entering Raqqada on 25 March 909 CE (296 AH), Abu Abdallah proclaimed an amnesty and reorganized coinage and Friday prayers ahead of his master's arrival.

2. Expedition to Sijilmasa and Release of al-Mahdi (909 CE)

  • Key Point: Abu Abdallah marched westward to Sijilmasa in southeastern Morocco to free the Ismaili imam Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi from local detention.

During this western campaign, Kutama troops also ended the Rustamid state at Tahert before escorting al-Mahdi triumphantly eastward to Ifriqiya.

3. Proclamation of the Fatimid Caliphate (909–910 CE)

  • Key Point: Entering Raqqada in January 910 CE, Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi assumed the title of Caliph and Commander of the Faithful.

Claiming descent through the Prophet's daughter Fatima, al-Mahdi established a rival caliphate to Baghdad. Shortly afterward (916–921 CE), he founded the fortified maritime port of al-Mahdiyya on the Tunisian coast as a defensible royal seat.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The founding of the Fatimid Caliphate shattered the political unity of a single caliphal title in the central Islamic lands. Operating from North Africa and Sicily, the Fatimids built a formidable Mediterranean navy and eventually conquered Egypt in 969 CE, where they founded Cairo and extended their influence into the Hijaz and Syria.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Chronological details of the Aghlabid collapse and Fatimid proclamation are drawn from Ibn al-Athir's Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, late third-century AH notices in Tarikh al-Tabari, and historical entries in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala.

929-khilafah-cordoba-diproklamasikan.title: Proclamation of the Caliphate of Cordoba
929-khilafah-cordoba-diproklamasikan.summary: Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed himself caliph in 929 CE, ushering in the political and cultural zenith of Umayyad Cordoba.
929-khilafah-cordoba-diproklamasikan.facts:
Date : January 929 CE (Dhu al-Hijjah 316 AH)
Location : Cordoba, Al-Andalus (modern Spain)
Key Figures : Abd al-Rahman III (al-Nasir li-Din Allah)
Outcome : Establishment of the Caliphate of Cordoba and golden age of Al-Andalus
Primary Sources : Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, ArchNet
929-khilafah-cordoba-diproklamasikan.body:
Context & Background

From 756 CE onward, Umayyad rulers in Al-Andalus contented themselves with the title of Amir, preserving the nominal ideal of a single Islamic caliphate. By the early tenth century, however, internal crises had weakened Abbasid authority in Baghdad, while the newly proclaimed Fatimid Caliphate in North Africa (909–910 CE) actively threatened Umayyad sea lanes and frontier allegiances.

When Abd al-Rahman III inherited the emirate in 912 CE, central authority was challenged by entrenched regional rebellions, most notably the long-running insurgency led by Umar ibn Hafsun at the mountain fortress of Bobastro alongside autonomous border lords in Toledo and Zaragoza.

Course of Events

1. Reunifying Al-Andalus (912–928 CE)

  • Key Point: Over seventeen years of disciplined campaigns and diplomacy, Abd al-Rahman III subdued rebel strongholds and restored central taxation and order.

The capture of Bobastro in 928 CE broke the backbone of domestic insurgency, consolidating Umayyad authority across southern and central Iberia and providing the political strength required to assert sovereign caliphal rank.

2. Assuming the Caliphal Title and Minting Gold Dinars (January 929 CE)

  • Key Point: On 16 January 929 CE (Dhu al-Hijjah 316 AH), Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed himself Caliph and Commander of the Faithful under the regnal name al-Nasir li-Din Allah.

Chancery decrees ordered his caliphal title recited in Friday sermons across Al-Andalus, while a state mint struck full-weight gold dinars bearing his name—asserting parity with both Baghdad and the Fatimids.

3. Founding Madinat al-Zahra and International Embassies (936–961 CE)

  • Key Point: Beginning in 936 CE, the caliph constructed the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahra west of Cordoba as an imperial administrative seat.

Featuring terraced gardens, aqueducts, and marble reception halls, Madinat al-Zahra hosted ambassadors from Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, northern Iberian kingdoms, and Holy Roman Emperor Otto I.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The 929 CE proclamation formally divided the tenth-century Islamic world into three competing caliphates—Abbasid, Fatimid, and Umayyad Cordoba. Under al-Nasir and his successor al-Hakam II, Cordoba flourished as one of Europe's largest and most literate metropolises, renowned for extensive libraries, public infrastructure, medicine, and architectural innovation.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative draws on fourth-century AH chronicles in Ibn al-Athir's Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, biographical notices in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, and urban architectural archives for Cordoba and Madinat al-Zahra at ArchNet.

969-kairo-didirikan.title: Founding of Cairo
969-kairo-didirikan.summary: The Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli conquered Egypt and founded Cairo in 969 CE as a new imperial capital along the Nile.
969-kairo-didirikan.facts:
Date : 969 CE (358 AH)
Location : Cairo, Egypt (northeast of Fustat)
Key Figures : Jawhar al-Siqilli, Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah
Outcome : Fatimid conquest of Egypt and establishment of al-Qahira (Cairo)
Primary Sources : Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, ArchNet
969-kairo-didirikan.body:
Context & Background

Since establishing power in Tunisia in 909 CE, the Fatimids had targeted Egypt as the strategic gateway to Red Sea commerce, Syria, and Iraq. Three early expeditions failed against Abbasid and Ikhshidid defenses, yet circumstances shifted dramatically after the death of Egypt's capable ruler Abu al-Misk Kafur in 968 CE.

Low Nile floods triggered severe famine and epidemics, while rival military factions paralyzed the Ikhshidid court. Local notables quietly invited Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah to intervene and restore stability.

Course of Events

1. Jawhar al-Siqilli's Expedition and Entry into Fustat (969 CE)

  • Key Point: General Jawhar al-Siqilli marched a well-provisioned army from Ifriqiya and secured Fustat in July 969 CE with minimal bloodshed.

Departing Kairouan in February 969 CE, Jawhar negotiated a formal charter of safety (aman) with Egyptian notables and dispersed remaining Ikhshidid resistance near Giza before entering Fustat in Sha'ban 358 AH.

2. Laying Out the Walled City of al-Qahira (969 CE)

  • Key Point: Rather than governing from crowded Fustat, Jawhar demarcated a rectangular walled royal enclosure northeast of the older city.

Originally called al-Mansuriyya, the mudbrick-walled city was renamed al-Qahira al-Mu'izziyya (The Victorious, modern Cairo) upon the caliph's arrival, housing royal regiments, ministries, and gates aligned along a central spine.

3. Royal Palaces and Arrival of Caliph al-Mu'izz (969–973 CE)

  • Key Point: Two monumental palaces flanked the central parade ground of Bayn al-Qasrayn, preparing the seat for Caliph al-Mu'izz's relocation in 973 CE.

After stabilizing Nile taxation and repelling Qarmatian raids from Syria, Jawhar welcomed Caliph al-Mu'izz in June 973 CE, permanently shifting the Fatimid capital from Tunisia to Egypt.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The founding of Cairo transformed Egypt into a major commercial bridge linking Indian Ocean spice routes via the Red Sea to Italian maritime republics across the Mediterranean. When Saladin ended Fatimid rule in 1171 CE, he enclosed Cairo, Fustat, and the Citadel within a unified urban framework that remains Egypt's capital today.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on year 358 AH accounts in Ibn al-Athir's Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, biographical profiles in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, and urban architectural surveys of Fatimid Cairo hosted by ArchNet.

970-al-azhar-didirikan.title: Founding of Al-Azhar
970-al-azhar-didirikan.summary: Constructed in Cairo in 970 CE, Al-Azhar Mosque evolved into a premier institution of Islamic scholarship that endures today.
970-al-azhar-didirikan.facts:
Date : 970–972 CE (359–361 AH)
Location : Cairo, Egypt
Key Figures : Jawhar al-Siqilli, Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, Ya'qub ibn Killis
Outcome : Establishment of Al-Azhar Mosque and its scholarly academy
Primary Sources : Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, ArchNet
970-al-azhar-didirikan.body:
Context & Background

Immediately after laying out the walls and royal palaces of Cairo in 969 CE, the Fatimids required a congregational mosque to anchor civic worship and state teaching alongside the older mosques of Amr ibn al-As in Fustat and Ibn Tulun.

Acting on Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah's directives, general Jawhar al-Siqilli selected a plot southeast of the royal palace complex to raise Al-Azhar Mosque, whose name evokes Fatima al-Zahra as well as the luminous palaces of the Fatimid court.

Course of Events

1. Foundation and Early Architecture (April 970 CE)

  • Key Point: Construction began on 4 April 970 CE (Jumada al-Ula 359 AH) following a hypostyle courtyard plan.

The original prayer hall featured five aisles parallel to the qibla wall, intersected by a wider raised central nave leading to the mihrab and opening onto a sunlit central courtyard (sahn) framed by pointed arches and marble columns.

2. Inaugural Friday Prayers (June 972 CE)

  • Key Point: Completed in just over two years, the mosque held its first Friday congregational prayer on 22 June 972 CE (7 Ramadan 361 AH).

Upon Caliph al-Mu'izz's arrival in Cairo in 973 CE, Al-Azhar served as the chief ceremonial mosque of the Fatimid capital.

3. Evolution into a Center of Higher Learning (975–988 CE)

  • Key Point: Organized legal lectures began in 975 CE under Chief Judge Ali ibn al-Nu'man and expanded into a salaried academy in 988 CE under Vizier Ya'qub ibn Killis.

During the reign of Caliph al-Aziz Billah, Ya'qub ibn Killis secured state stipends and residential quarters for dozens of resident jurists and students, establishing structured study circles covering jurisprudence, Arabic grammar, logic, history, and astronomy.

Historical Impact & Legacy

After Saladin ended Fatimid rule in 1171 CE, Friday prayers shifted temporarily away from Al-Azhar until Mamluk Sultan Baybars revived the mosque in 1266 CE as a preeminent Sunni seminary. Following the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 CE, displaced scholars flocked to Cairo, cementing Al-Azhar's status as one of the world's longest-running universities into the modern age.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative is informed by fourth-century AH events in Ibn al-Athir's Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, scholarly profiles in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, and architectural surveys of Al-Azhar Mosque archived by ArchNet.

1011-ibnu-al-haitham-dan-ilmu-optik.title: Ibn al-Haytham and Optics
1011-ibnu-al-haitham-dan-ilmu-optik.summary: Working in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham authored the Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir), pioneering controlled experimentation in scientific inquiry.
1011-ibnu-al-haitham-dan-ilmu-optik.facts:
Date : c. 1011–1021 CE
Location : Cairo, Egypt (born in Basra, Iraq)
Key Figures : Al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), Caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah
Key Work : Kitab al-Manazir (Book of Optics)
Primary Sources : Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, ArchNet
1011-ibnu-al-haitham-dan-ilmu-optik.body:
Context & Background

Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham—known in medieval Europe as Alhazen—was born in Basra around 965 CE and gained renown across Iraq for his mastery of mathematics, astronomy, and physics. Word reached Egypt that he believed he could design a hydraulic structure to regulate the annual flooding of the Nile.

Fatimid Caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah invited him to Cairo to carry out the project. However, after inspecting the river upstream toward Aswan and examining monumental ancient ruins along its banks, Ibn al-Haytham concluded that damming the massive Nile exceeded the engineering means of his era.

Course of Events

1. Withdrawal Near Al-Azhar Mosque (c. 1011 CE)

  • Key Point: Fearing Caliph al-Hakim's unpredictable wrath after admitting the Nile project was unfeasible, Ibn al-Haytham stepped back from court service into seclusion.

Biographical accounts relate that he lived quietly in a small dwelling near the gate of Al-Azhar Mosque between roughly 1011 and al-Hakim's death in 1021 CE, supporting himself by copying manuscripts of Euclid, Ptolemy, and Apollonius while conducting optical experiments.

2. Refuting Emission Theory in Kitab al-Manazir (1011–1021 CE)

  • Key Point: In his seven-volume Kitab al-Manazir (Book of Optics), Ibn al-Haytham overturned the ancient theory of Euclid and Ptolemy that vision occurs via rays emitted from the eye.

Observing solar glare and projecting light through a dark chamber (al-bayt al-muzlim / camera obscura), he demonstrated that light travels in straight lines from illuminated objects into the eye, forming visual perception within the optical apparatus and brain.

3. Controlled Experiments and the Method of I'tibar

  • Key Point: Ibn al-Haytham formalized i'tibar—systematic testing with repeatable experimental setups to verify mathematical hypotheses.

He measured reflection on curved mirrors, investigated refraction through water and glass, and even estimated the thickness of Earth's atmosphere by analyzing twilight angles.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Kitab al-Manazir redefined optics for centuries. In the Islamic world, Kamal al-Din al-Farisi built on his work to explain the physics of rainbows. Translated into Latin as De Aspectibus or Perspectiva around 1200 CE, Ibn al-Haytham's treatise profoundly shaped Roger Bacon, Witelo, Johannes Kepler, and the rise of modern experimental science.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Historical context for early fifth-century AH Cairo under al-Hakim is drawn from Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, scholarly biographies in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, and architectural surveys of Fatimid Cairo around Al-Azhar at ArchNet.

1037-wafatnya-ibnu-sina.title: Death of Ibn Sina
1037-wafatnya-ibnu-sina.summary: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), physician and philosopher who authored the Canon of Medicine (Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb), died in Hamadan in 1037 CE.
1037-wafatnya-ibnu-sina.facts:
Date : June 1037 CE (Ramadan 428 AH)
Location : Hamadan, Persia (western Iran)
Key Figures : Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Sina (Avicenna), Ala al-Dawla
Key Works : Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, Kitab al-Shifa
Primary Sources : Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala
1037-wafatnya-ibnu-sina.body:
Context & Background

Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abdallah ibn Sina—known in Europe as Avicenna—was born around 980 CE near Bukhara (modern Uzbekistan) under Samanid rule. Having earned court favor as a young physician with access to the Samanid royal library, he faced displacement when the dynasty collapsed at the turn of the millennium.

Ibn Sina spent decades moving among rival courts in Persia, serving as physician and vizier to Buyid ruler Shams al-Dawla in Hamadan—where political intrigue briefly landed him in prison—and later as a respected adviser to Kakuyid ruler Ala al-Dawla Muhammad in Isfahan.

Course of Events

1. Completion of Monumental Works in Persia (1015–1036 CE)

  • Key Point: Amid state duties and frequent travel between Hamadan and Isfahan, Ibn Sina completed his masterworks Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine) and Kitab al-Shifa.

Organizing Greek, Persian, and Islamic clinical knowledge into five systematic volumes, Al-Qanun laid out clear rules for testing pharmacological efficacy, contagious disease quarantine, and bedside diagnostics, while Kitab al-Shifa spanned logic, physics, mathematics, and metaphysics.

2. Severe Colic During the March to Hamadan (1037 CE)

  • Key Point: Accompanying Ala al-Dawla on an expedition toward Hamadan in early 1037 CE, Ibn Sina suffered a severe recurrence of chronic intestinal colic.

Exhaustion and overly aggressive self-administered remedies worsened his condition upon reaching Hamadan, prompting him to cease harsh treatments as his strength faded.

3. Passing and Burial in Hamadan (June 1037 CE)

  • Key Point: Ibn Sina died in Hamadan in Ramadan 428 AH (June 1037 CE) at roughly fifty-seven years of age.

According to his pupil Abu Ubayd al-Juzjani, in his final days he bathed, gave his wealth to charity, emancipated his enslaved attendants, and recited the Qur'an continuously until his passing, after which he was buried in Hamadan.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona in the twelfth century as the Canon Medicinae, Ibn Sina's medical encyclopedia became one of the most printed medical texts after Gutenberg and served as a core university textbook in Bologna, Montpellier, Paris, and Louvain—as well as across the Islamic world—until the late seventeenth century.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on events recorded under 428 AH in Ibn al-Athir's Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and the biographical entry detailing Ibn Sina's career and final days in al-Dhahabi's Siyar A'lam al-Nubala.

1055-seljuk-memasuki-baghdad.title: Seljuk Entry into Baghdad
1055-seljuk-memasuki-baghdad.summary: Tughril Beg of the Seljuk Dynasty entered Baghdad in 1055 CE, ending Buyid dominance and establishing Seljuk protection over the Abbasid Caliphate.
1055-seljuk-memasuki-baghdad.body:
Context & Background

By the mid-eleventh century, the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad had long lost independent military command. Since 945 CE, the Shi'i Buyid emirs had exercised real political and military authority over Iraq, confining Caliph al-Qa'im bi-Amrillah to ceremonial and religious oversight. As Buyid factions fell into internal rivalry, the Turkish military commander Arslan al-Basasiri forged ties with the Fatimid Caliphate in Cairo, threatening to shift Baghdad's allegiance away from the Abbasids.

Further east, the Oghuz Turkic Seljuk confederation had risen to prominence after defeating the Ghaznavids at the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040 CE. Under Tughril Beg, Seljuk forces consolidated control over Nishapur, Rayy, and Isfahan. Seeking a Sunni counterweight to both the waning Buyids and Fatimid encroachment, Caliph al-Qa'im dispatched envoys inviting Tughril Beg to march on Baghdad and restore Abbasid stability.

Course of Events

1. Caliphal Invitation and Seljuk Arrival (December 1055 CE)

Tughril Beg marched westward from Persia into Iraq in late 1055 CE (Ramadan 447 AH). Prior to his arrival, Friday sermons across Baghdad began invoking Tughril Beg's name alongside the caliph, signaling formal recognition from the Abbasid court. In mid-December 1055, Seljuk cavalry encamped along the eastern banks of the Tigris River and entered the capital with caliphal escorts.

  • Key Point: Invoking Tughril Beg in the Friday khutbah marked the formal transfer of Baghdad's military patronage from the Buyids to the Seljuk Dynasty.

2. Arrest of the Last Buyid Emir

Friction quickly flared between Seljuk troops and Baghdad's populace and remaining Buyid units over quartering and market supplies. Responding to the unrest, Tughril Beg detained the last Buyid ruler, al-Malik al-Rahim, along with senior Buyid officers in late December 1055. This decisive step terminated 110 years of Buyid rule in Iraq.

  • Key Point: The capture of al-Malik al-Rahim permanently ended Buyid governance in Baghdad and placed Iraq's military administration under Seljuk authority.

3. Al-Basasiri's Revolt and Seljuk Restoration (1058–1060 CE)

Seljuk control faced an immediate test when Tughril Beg marched back to Persia to suppress a rebellion by his half-brother Ibrahim Inal. In late 1058, Arslan al-Basasiri seized Baghdad with Fatimid financial backing, exiled Caliph al-Qa'im to Haditha, and proclaimed the Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir in the capital's mosques for nearly a year. After crushing the uprising in Persia, Tughril Beg returned in December 1059, reinstated al-Qa'im, and defeated and killed al-Basasiri near Kufa in early 1060.

  • Key Point: Tughril Beg's 1060 campaign secured the Abbasid seat in Baghdad and halted Fatimid political expansion into Mesopotamia.

Impact & Historical Legacy

The entry of the Seljuks into Baghdad institutionalized a dual-authority framework in medieval Islamic governance: the Abbasid Caliph served as the source of religious and legal legitimacy, while the Seljuk Sultan wielded sovereign military and administrative power. Caliph al-Qa'im conferred upon Tughril Beg the titles Rukn al-Din and Malik al-Mashriq wa al-Maghrib (King of the East and West), sealed by dynastic marriage. This political alignment funded major Sunni scholarly institutions such as the Nizamiyya Madrasa under Alp Arslan and Nizam al-Mulk and enabled Seljuk expansion into Syria and Anatolia.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This account of the 447 AH / 1055 CE Seljuk entry into Baghdad draws on Ibn al-Athir's primary chronicle in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and Imam al-Dhahabi's biographical entries in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'. Urban and architectural contexts of Seljuk Iraq and Persia are referenced through ArchNet. Events and figures are documented strictly from historical chronicles without fictional embellishment.
1055-seljuk-memasuki-baghdad.facts:
Date : December 1055 CE / Ramadan 447 AH
Location : Baghdad, Iraq
Key Figures : Tughril Beg, Caliph al-Qa'im bi-Amrillah, al-Malik al-Rahim, Arslan al-Basasiri
Parties Involved : Seljuk Sultanate, Abbasid Caliphate, Buyid Dynasty, Fatimid-backed Factions
Significance : End of Buyid rule in Baghdad and establishment of Seljuk military patronage over the Abbasid Caliphate

1071-pertempuran-manzikert.title: Battle of Manzikert
1071-pertempuran-manzikert.summary: Sultan Alp Arslan of the Seljuks defeated Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert in 1071 CE, opening Anatolia to Turkic settlement.
1071-pertempuran-manzikert.body:
Context & Background

Throughout the 1060s, Turkmen cavalry bands allied with the Great Seljuk Empire conducted frequent raids into Byzantine Armenia and eastern Anatolia. Following Tughril Beg's death in 1063 CE, his nephew Sultan Alp Arslan took power, capturing Ani in 1064 and pushing deep toward Caesarea. To halt these incursions and reassert imperial frontiers, Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes marched east from Constantinople in the spring of 1071 at the head of a large multi-ethnic force composed of Byzantine regulars, Norman mercenaries, Varangian guards, and Pecheneg and Oghuz auxiliaries.

Romanos IV aimed to reclaim key fortresses near Lake Van, including Manzikert (modern Malazgirt) and Akhlat. Sultan Alp Arslan, who was campaigning near Aleppo against Fatimid-aligned territories, turned swiftly northward upon learning of the imperial advance.

Course of Events

1. Convergence Near Lake Van

In August 1071, Romanos IV retook Manzikert and detached a major portion of his troops to besiege Akhlat. This division of forces created an opening for Alp Arslan, who approached rapidly via Azerbaijan with core Seljuk cavalry and local levies. Envoys from Alp Arslan proposed a truce, but Romanos IV rejected it unless the Seljuks surrendered major frontier bases, ending diplomatic talks.

  • Key Point: Splitting the Byzantine army toward Akhlat and rejecting Seljuk truce terms left Romanos IV vulnerable on the plain of Manzikert.

2. Steppe Tactics and Engagement (26 August 1071 CE)

On Friday, 26 August 1071 (27 Dhu al-Qi'dah 463 AH), the armies clashed south of Manzikert. Alp Arslan wore white burial garments before addressing his troops and designating his son Malik-Shah as heir. Seljuk horse archers deployed classic steppe tactics: showering advancing Byzantine ranks with arrows while executing feigned retreats to draw the heavy infantry away from their fortified camp.

As dusk settled, Romanos IV ordered an orderly withdrawal back toward camp. Miscommunication in the rear lines allowed political rival Andronikos Doukas, commander of the reserve, to retreat from the field while spreading rumors of the emperor's death. Concurrently, several Oghuz Turkic mercenaries in Byzantine service defected to Alp Arslan's side.

  • Key Point: Feigned-retreat archery and the sudden withdrawal of the Byzantine reserve shattered imperial cohesion at nightfall.

3. Capture of Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes

Surrounded with his personal guard, Romanos IV fought on until his horse collapsed and his hand was wounded. Taken prisoner by a Seljuk soldier, he became the first reigning Byzantine emperor ever captured in battle by a Muslim ruler.

  • Key Point: The capture of Romanos IV broke the central military command of the Byzantine Empire in eastern Anatolia.

Impact & Historical Legacy

Alp Arslan treated Romanos IV with courtesy and released him under a treaty stipulating ransom, annual tribute, and border concessions. However, while Romanos returned westward, the Doukas faction deposed and blinded him in 1072, invalidating the agreement. Ensuing Byzantine civil wars left the Taurus and Anatolian frontier defenses unmanned. Over the following decade, Turkmen groups migrated across the Anatolian plateau, founding the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum and transforming Anatolia's demographic and cultural landscape, while imperial appeals to Rome helped precipitate the First Crusade.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This historical synthesis of the 463 AH / 1071 CE Battle of Manzikert relies on Ibn al-Athir's chronicle in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and Imam al-Dhahabi's biographical account of Alp Arslan in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'. Architectural heritage of subsequent Anatolian Seljuk settlements is referenced via ArchNet.
1071-pertempuran-manzikert.facts:
Date : 26 August 1071 CE / 27 Dhu al-Qi'dah 463 AH
Location : Manzikert (Malazgirt), Eastern Anatolia
Key Figures : Sultan Alp Arslan, Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes, Andronikos Doukas
Parties Involved : Great Seljuk Empire vs Byzantine Empire
Significance : Decisive Seljuk victory that collapsed Byzantine eastern defenses and opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement

1096-perang-salib-pertama.title: The First Crusade
1096-perang-salib-pertama.summary: European Crusader forces marched eastward between 1096 and 1099 CE, exploiting Seljuk fragmentation to establish Crusader states across the Levant.
1096-perang-salib-pertama.body:
Context & Background

Following the deaths of Grand Vizier Nizam al-Mulk and Sultan Malik-Shah I in 1092 CE, the Great Seljuk Empire fractured into competing succession states. Syria and Iraq splintered among rival rulers—Barkiyaruq, Ridwan in Aleppo, Duqaq in Damascus, and Kilij Arslan I in Anatolia—while Fatimid Egypt held coastal Palestine. Into this divided landscape came Pope Urban II's call at the Council of Clermont in November 1095, responding to Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos's appeals for military aid while directing European nobles toward Jerusalem.

An early disorganized wave, the People's Crusade under Peter the Hermit, crossed into Anatolia in 1096 and was annihilated by Kilij Arslan I near Civetot in October 1096. This rapid victory led Anatolian Seljuk commanders to underestimate the far larger aristocratic armies arriving the following year.

Course of Events

1. Crossing Anatolia and Fall of Nicaea (1097 CE)

In spring 1097, the main Princes' Crusade—led by Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto, Raymond of Toulouse, and Baldwin of Boulogne—assembled at Constantinople and crossed the Bosphorus. While Kilij Arslan I was campaigning eastward against the Danishmendids, Crusaders besieged his capital at Nicaea, which surrendered to Byzantine envoys in June 1097. On 1 July 1097, Crusader forces defeated Kilij Arslan's field army at Dorylaeum, opening the overland corridor across Anatolia.

  • Key Point: The loss of Nicaea and defeat at Dorylaeum forced Kilij Arslan I onto the defensive and left the route to northern Syria open.

2. Founding of Edessa and Siege of Antioch (1097–1098 CE)

Detaching eastward in Cilicia, Baldwin of Boulogne seized Edessa in March 1098, creating the first Crusader state. Meanwhile, the main army besieged Antioch from October 1097 to June 1098 amidst severe famine on both sides. Aided by a treacherous tower guard, Bohemond's men breached the walls on 3 June 1098. A Muslim relief coalition under Kerbogha of Mosul soon besieged the Crusaders inside Antioch, but internal rivalries among Syrian and Iraqi commanders fractured the relief army, allowing the Crusaders to rout it on 28 June 1098.

  • Key Point: Antioch's fall and the collapse of Kerbogha's relief coalition cemented Crusader control over northern Syria.

3. March South Through the Levant (1098–1099 CE)

After storming Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in late 1098, the Crusaders marched southward along the Levantine coast. Isolated local rulers and Fatimid coastal garrisons lacked coordinated reinforcement from Baghdad or Cairo, enabling the Crusader army to reach Palestine by June 1099 largely unopposed.

  • Key Point: Deep political divisions between Seljuk Syria and Fatimid Egypt left the Levantine corridor exposed to the final advance on Jerusalem.

Impact & Historical Legacy

The First Crusade carved four Latin principalities out of the Levant: the County of Edessa (1098), Principality of Antioch (1098), Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099), and County of Tripoli (1109). This presence reshaped Middle Eastern geopolitics for nearly two centuries, disrupting inland-coastal trade and prompting gradual Muslim counter-unification under the Zengids—Imad ad-Din Zengi and Nur ad-Din Mahmud—and later Salahuddin al-Ayyubi.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This history of the First Crusade (489–492 AH / 1096–1099 CE) draws upon Ibn al-Athir's contemporary political chronicle in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and Imam al-Dhahabi's biographical records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', alongside architectural documentation of Levantine fortresses via ArchNet.
1096-perang-salib-pertama.facts:
Date : 1096–1099 CE / 489–492 AH
Location : Anatolia, Northern Syria, Levantine Coast, Palestine
Key Figures : Kilij Arslan I, Kerbogha of Mosul, Pope Urban II, Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto
Parties Involved : Western European Crusader Armies & Byzantine Empire vs Anatolian-Syrian Seljuk Emirates & Fatimid Garrisons
Significance : Establishment of the Crusader states in the Levant and onset of two centuries of military-political confrontation

1099-yerusalem-jatuh-ke-tangan-pasukan-s.title: Fall of Jerusalem to the Crusaders
1099-yerusalem-jatuh-ke-tangan-pasukan-s.summary: Crusader armies breached the walls of Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 CE after a five-week siege, massacring inhabitants and establishing the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
1099-yerusalem-jatuh-ke-tangan-pasukan-s.body:
Context & Background

In August 1098 CE, the Fatimid vizier al-Afdal Shahanshah had recaptured Jerusalem from its Artuqid Turkmen governors. Less than a year later, the main First Crusade army—having consolidated Antioch—marched down the Levantine coast unopposed by fractured Syrian Seljuk emirs or delayed Egyptian forces. On 7 June 1099, between 12,000 and 15,000 Crusader fighters led by Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Toulouse, Tancred, and Robert of Normandy invested Jerusalem. Fatimid governor Iftikhar ad-Dawla commanded a modest garrison, poisoning outer wells and bringing livestock inside the walls to withstand a siege.

Course of Events

1. Supply Shortages and Siege Towers (June–July 1099 CE)

Early assaults faltered under summer heat and acute water shortages; a premature attack on 13 June failed for lack of scaling ladders. The balance shifted in mid-June when Genoese ships docked at Jaffa with provisions, timber, and skilled engineers who dismantled vessels to construct two large wheeled siege towers and stone-throwing engines.

  • Key Point: Genoese naval supplies and timber from Jaffa enabled the Crusaders to build decisive siege towers against Jerusalem's walls.

2. Breach of the Northern Wall (13–15 July 1099 CE)

On 10 July, Godfrey of Bouillon shifted his siege tower quietly to a weaker stretch of the northern wall near Herod's Gate, while Raymond of Toulouse pressed the southern sector at Mount Zion. Sustained bombardment and ditch-filling began on 13 July. At midday on Friday, 15 July 1099 (22 Sha'ban 492 AH), Godfrey's troops lowered a wooden bridge onto the northern rampart, broke into the city, and opened the gates.

  • Key Point: On 15 July 1099, Godfrey of Bouillon's troops breached the northern wall and opened Jerusalem to the Crusader host.

3. Massacre of Citizens and Surrender of David's Tower

Once inside, Crusader forces carried out a two-day massacre of Muslim and Jewish civilians across the city. Thousands who sought shelter inside the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound were killed, and the city's Jewish community perished in their burning synagogue. Governor Iftikhar ad-Dawla surrendered David's Tower to Raymond of Toulouse under safe-conduct to Ascalon. On 12 August 1099, Crusaders defeated a tardy Fatimid relief army at Ascalon.

  • Key Point: The storming of Jerusalem ended in a widespread massacre at Al-Aqsa and terminated Muslim rule over the city for 88 years.

Impact & Historical Legacy

The conquest ended 461 years of continuous Islamic administration since Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab's peaceful pact in 638 CE. Godfrey assumed rule as Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri; Al-Aqsa Mosque became the royal residence and later Knights Templar headquarters, while the Dome of the Rock was converted into a church. Reports of the slaughter resonated across Damascus and Baghdad—recorded by Ibn al-Athir and poets like al-Abiwardi—and became the central rallying cause for Zengi, Nur ad-Din, and Salahuddin al-Ayyubi.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This account of the fall of Jerusalem on 22 Sha'ban 492 AH / 15 July 1099 CE relies on Ibn al-Athir's chronicle in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and Imam al-Dhahabi's historical narrative in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'. Architectural history of the Haram al-Sharif and Jerusalem fortifications is referenced via ArchNet.
1099-yerusalem-jatuh-ke-tangan-pasukan-s.facts:
Date : 15 July 1099 CE / 22 Sha'ban 492 AH
Location : Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), Palestine
Key Figures : Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Toulouse, Tancred, Iftikhar ad-Dawla
Parties Involved : First Crusade Armies vs Fatimid Caliphate Garrison
Significance : Creation of the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem and 88-year interruption of Muslim governance over the city

1111-wafatnya-al-ghazali.title: Death of Al-Ghazali
1111-wafatnya-al-ghazali.summary: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, author of Ihya' Ulum al-Din and leading scholar of the Seljuk era, passed away in Thus, Khurasan, in December 1111 CE.
1111-wafatnya-al-ghazali.body:
Context & Background

Born in 450 AH / 1058 CE in Thus, Khurasan, Abu Hamid Muhammad al-Ghazali studied under the renowned jurist-theologian Imam al-Haramain al-Juwaini in Nishapur. His mastery of Shafi'i jurisprudence and Ash'ari theology brought him into the circle of Seljuk Grand Vizier Nizam al-Mulk, who appointed him chief professor at the Nizamiyya Madrasa in Baghdad in 1091 CE (484 AH). Over four years in Baghdad, al-Ghazali authored major philosophical analyses including Maqasid al-Falasifah and Tahafut al-Falasifah (The Incoherence of the Philosophers), establishing himself as the preeminent Sunni scholar of his age.

Yet at the height of academic acclaim, he fell into a severe spiritual crisis, questioning whether career prestige corrupted scholarly sincerity and realizing that formal dialectics alone could not yield inward certainty.

Course of Events

1. Departure from Nizamiyya Baghdad (1095 CE)

In late 1095 CE (Dhu al-Qi'dah 488 AH), al-Ghazali resigned from his Baghdad chair, citing pilgrimage to Mecca as his outward reason, and left his official posts behind. He later documented this turning point in his intellectual autobiography, Al-Munqidh min al-Dalal (Deliverance from Error).

  • Key Point: Leaving Baghdad in 1095 CE shifted al-Ghazali's life from state-sponsored scholastic debate toward spiritual purification and religious renewal.

2. Ten Years of Seclusion and Ihya' Ulum al-Din

For roughly ten years (1095–1105 CE), al-Ghazali lived quietly in Damascus, Jerusalem, Hebron, Mecca, and Medina. During this retreat, he composed his monumental Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din (The Revival of the Religious Sciences), integrating Islamic law, worship, social ethics, and spiritual discipline grounded in the Qur'an and Sunnah.

  • Key Point: His decade of seclusion across Syria and the Hijaz produced Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din, bridging outward jurisprudence with inward sincerity.

3. Return to Nishapur and Passing in Thus (18 December 1111 CE)

In 1106 CE, Seljuk Vizier Fakhr al-Mulk persuaded al-Ghazali to resume teaching at the Nizamiyya Madrasa in Nishapur, where he completed his legal-theory treatise Al-Mustasfa. He soon retired to his native Tabaran in Thus, founding a local madrasa and spiritual retreat. At dawn on Monday, 14 Jumada al-Akhirah 505 AH (18 December 1111 CE), he performed ablution, asked for his shroud, and passed away peacefully at age 53.

  • Key Point: After briefly teaching in Nishapur, al-Ghazali retired to Thus and died peacefully on 18 December 1111 CE.

Impact & Historical Legacy

Remembered as Hujjat al-Islam (Proof of Islam), al-Ghazali anchored Sunni orthodoxy by uniting Shafi'i jurisprudence, Ash'ari theology, Aristotelian logic in legal reasoning, and Sharia-bound Sufism. His critique of metaphysics sparked enduring philosophical debate—most famously answered by Ibn Rushd in Tahafut al-Tahafut—while Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din shaped curricula from Cairo to Southeast Asian pesantrens for centuries.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This biographical account of al-Ghazali's life and passing in 505 AH / 1111 CE is sourced from Imam al-Dhahabi's extensive biography in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' and Ibn al-Athir's annalistic entry in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh. Architectural history of Seljuk Khurasan and the Nizamiyya institutions is referenced via ArchNet.
1111-wafatnya-al-ghazali.facts:
Date : 18 December 1111 CE / 14 Jumada al-Akhirah 505 AH
Location : Tabaran, Thus, Khurasan (Iran)
Key Figures : Abu Hamid Muhammad al-Ghazali, Imam al-Haramain al-Juwaini, Nizam al-Mulk, Fakhr al-Mulk
Major Works : Ihya' Ulum al-Din, Tahafut al-Falasifah, Al-Munqidh min al-Dalal, Al-Mustasfa
Significance : Honored as Hujjat al-Islam for synthesizing Sunni jurisprudence, Ash'ari theology, logic, and ethical Sufism

1187-salahuddin-al-ayyubi-merebut-yerusa.title: Salahuddin al-Ayyubi Captures Jerusalem
1187-salahuddin-al-ayyubi-merebut-yerusa.summary: Following his decisive victory at Hattin in 1187 CE, Salahuddin reclaimed Jerusalem peacefully through negotiated terms protecting the city's inhabitants.
1187-salahuddin-al-ayyubi-merebut-yerusa.body:
Context & Background

After nearly nine decades of Crusader rule in Jerusalem, the unification of Syria and Egypt initiated by Imad ad-Din Zengi and Nur ad-Din Mahmud culminated under Sultan Salahuddin Yusuf ibn Ayyub. Having ended the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt (1171 CE) and united Damascus, Aleppo, and Mosul under Ayyubid rule, Salahuddin confronted the Kingdom of Jerusalem following Raynald of Chatillon's truce violations against merchant and pilgrim caravans.

The military turning point came on 4 July 1187 (24 Rabi' al-Akhir 583 AH) at the Battle of Hattin near Lake Tiberias, where Ayyubid forces encircled the Crusader field army and captured King Guy of Lusignan. Within two months, Acre, Nablus, Jaffa, Gaza, and Ascalon fell, isolating Jerusalem from coastal reinforcement.

Course of Events

1. Initial Siege and Shift to the Northern Wall (September 1187 CE)

Salahuddin's forces surrounded Jerusalem on 20 September 1187 (15 Rajab 583 AH). Inside, Balian of Ibelin organized citizens and remaining knights to hold the walls. For five days, Ayyubid troops probed the western fortifications near David's Tower before Salahuddin relocated his siege engines and sappers on 25 September to the northern wall near the Mount of Olives—the exact sector breached by Crusaders in 1099.

  • Key Point: Shifting siege batteries to the northern wall on 25 September enabled Ayyubid sappers to undermine the fortress foundations.

2. Breach and Negotiated Capitulation

Covered by archers and mangonels, Ayyubid sappers collapsed a section of the northern rampart on 29 September. Facing imminent assault, Balian sought terms, warning that defenders would destroy the Islamic shrines and slay Muslim captives if denied quarter. Prioritizing the sanctuaries and civilian lives, Salahuddin accepted a ransom arrangement (10 dinars per man, 5 per woman, 1 per child), personally and with his brother al-Malik al-'Adil freeing thousands of impoverished citizens.

  • Key Point: Negotiated surrender spared Jerusalem from bloodshed and safeguarded the Al-Aqsa sanctuary and civilian population.

3. Peaceful Entry on 27 Rajab 583 AH (2 October 1187 CE)

On Friday, 2 October 1187—corresponding to 27 Rajab 583 AH, the commemoration of Isra' and Mi'raj—Salahuddin entered Jerusalem in orderly procession. Unlike the 1099 massacre, no looting or retaliatory slaughter occurred; Ayyubid guards escorted departing Latin residents safely toward the coast.

  • Key Point: Salahuddin's entry on 27 Rajab 583 AH restored Jerusalem to Muslim rule without reprisals against civilians.

Impact & Historical Legacy

Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock were purified and restored to Islamic worship, adorned with the intricately carved wooden minbar commissioned by Nur ad-Din in Aleppo, while Qadi Muhyiddin ibn al-Zaki delivered the first Friday sermon. Eastern Christians were permitted to stay, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre remained intact under neutral custody. News of Jerusalem's fall triggered Europe's mobilization for the Third Crusade in 1189.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This account of the 583 AH / 1187 CE liberation of Jerusalem relies on Ibn al-Athir's contemporary chronicle in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and Imam al-Dhahabi's biography of Salahuddin in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', with Ayyubid architectural preservation at Al-Aqsa referenced through ArchNet.
1187-salahuddin-al-ayyubi-merebut-yerusa.facts:
Date : 2 October 1187 CE / 27 Rajab 583 AH
Location : Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), Palestine
Key Figures : Salahuddin al-Ayyubi, al-Malik al-'Adil, Balian of Ibelin, Muhyiddin ibn al-Zaki
Parties Involved : Ayyubid Sultanate vs Kingdom of Jerusalem
Significance : Peaceful restoration of Jerusalem to Muslim rule after 88 years and protection of residents and religious sites

1192-perjanjian-ramla.title: Treaty of Ramla
1192-perjanjian-ramla.summary: Salahuddin and King Richard I of England signed the Treaty of Ramla in September 1192 CE, ending the Third Crusade, preserving Muslim sovereignty over Jerusalem, and granting safe passage to unarmed Christian pilgrims.
1192-perjanjian-ramla.body:
Context & Background

Salahuddin's liberation of Jerusalem in 1187 prompted Europe's Third Crusade, led by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II of France, and Richard I of England. After Barbarossa drowned in 1190 and Acre fell to the Crusaders in July 1191, Philip returned to France, leaving Richard I in sole command. Richard defeated Salahuddin's field forces along the coast at Arsuf on 7 September 1191 and refortified Jaffa. Twice over 1191–1192, Richard advanced near the Judean hills toward Jerusalem, yet halted both times because fragile supply lines from the coast made holding an inland city untenable. Meanwhile, after five years of uninterrupted warfare, Salahuddin's Ayyubid forces also required respite and fiscal recovery.

Course of Events

1. Final Clashes at Jaffa (July–August 1192 CE)

When talks stalled in July 1192, Salahuddin stormed Jaffa's lower town while the citadel held out. Sailing quickly from Acre, Richard relieved Jaffa and repulsed Ayyubid counterattacks in early August 1192. The coastal stalemate convinced both commanders that decisive military victory remained out of reach.

  • Key Point: The August 1192 standoff at Jaffa underscored a strategic equilibrium that returned both rulers to diplomacy.

2. Diplomacy of Al-Malik al-'Adil and Signing (2 September 1192 CE)

Extended negotiations were mediated largely by Salahuddin's brother, al-Malik al-'Adil, who built a working rapport with Richard I. On 2 September 1192 (22 Sha'ban 588 AH), envoys ratified the Treaty of Ramla (also signed at Jaffa), establishing a three-year and eight-month truce.

  • Key Point: Shuttle diplomacy led by al-Malik al-'Adil sealed the Treaty of Ramla on 2 September 1192 CE, closing the Third Crusade.

3. Core Clauses of the Truce

Under the treaty, Jerusalem and inland Palestine and Syria remained firmly under Ayyubid sovereignty. The Crusaders kept a narrow coastal strip stretching from Tyre to Jaffa, centered at Acre, while the fortifications of Ascalon were demolished to prevent future threats toward Egypt or Jerusalem. In return, Salahuddin guaranteed safe passage for unarmed Christian pilgrims and European merchants visiting Jerusalem.

  • Key Point: The agreement affirmed Ayyubid control of Jerusalem, Crusader coastal ports from Tyre to Jaffa, the dismantling of Ascalon, and pilgrim access.

Impact & Historical Legacy

The Treaty of Ramla spared Jerusalem from a second siege in five years and stabilized Mediterranean commerce between Egypt, Syria, and Italian maritime republics. Richard sailed for Europe in October 1192, while Salahuddin inspected Palestinian defenses and returned to Damascus, where he passed away six months later in March 1193 (27 Safar 589 AH).

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This history of the 588 AH / 1192 CE Treaty of Ramla draws on Ibn al-Athir's contemporary narrative in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and Imam al-Dhahabi's biographical records of Salahuddin and al-Malik al-'Adil in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', with Ayyubid coastal fortifications referenced via ArchNet.
1192-perjanjian-ramla.facts:
Date : 2 September 1192 CE / 22 Sha'ban 588 AH
Location : Ramla and Jaffa, Palestine
Key Figures : Salahuddin al-Ayyubi, al-Malik al-'Adil, King Richard I of England
Parties Involved : Ayyubid Sultanate vs Third Crusade Forces
Significance : Ended the Third Crusade, affirmed Muslim sovereignty over Jerusalem, and secured safe passage for unarmed Christian pilgrims

1198-wafatnya-ibnu-rusyd.title: Death of Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
1198-wafatnya-ibnu-rusyd.summary: Andalusian jurist, physician, and philosopher Ibn Rushd (Averroes) died in Marrakesh in December 1198 CE, leaving enduring legacies in Islamic jurisprudence and European thought.
1198-wafatnya-ibnu-rusyd.body:
Context & Background

Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Rushd—known in Latin Europe as Averroes—was born in Cordoba in 1126 CE (520 AH) to a prominent family of Maliki judges. Trained in jurisprudence, medicine, and philosophy, he served as qadi of Seville (1169) and chief qadi of Cordoba (1171), as well as court physician to Almohad Caliphs Abu Ya'qub Yusuf and Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur.

His output spanned comparative Islamic law (Bidayat al-Mujtahid), medical theory (Al-Kulliyyat fi al-Tibb), legal-philosophical methodology (Fasl al-Maqal), his rebuttal to al-Ghazali (Tahafut al-Tahafut), and exhaustive commentaries on Aristotle.

Course of Events

1. Political Pressure and Exile to Lucena (1195 CE)

In 1195 CE (591 AH), as Caliph Ya'qub al-Mansur prepared for a major campaign against Castile culminating at the Battle of Alarcos, opposition from conservative legal factions in Cordoba intensified against philosophical study. Seeking scholarly unity ahead of war, al-Mansur ordered Ibn Rushd exiled to Lucena near Cordoba and banned philosophical treatises while sparing works on medicine, arithmetic, and astronomy.

  • Key Point: Ibn Rushd's brief 1195 exile to Lucena reflected wartime political concessions to traditionalist factions before the Battle of Alarcos.

2. Rehabilitation in Marrakesh

After returning victorious from Iberia to the Almohad capital of Marrakesh, Caliph al-Mansur received petitions from Seville's notables on Ibn Rushd's behalf. Around 1197–1198 CE, the caliph rescinded the ban, summoned Ibn Rushd to Marrakesh, and restored his standing at court.

  • Key Point: Caliph al-Mansur rehabilitated Ibn Rushd at the Marrakesh court prior to the scholar's final months.

3. Passing in Marrakesh and Reburial in Cordoba (10 December 1198 CE)

On 9 Safar 595 AH (10 December 1198 CE), Ibn Rushd died in Marrakesh around age 72 and was interred outside Bab Taghzut. Three months later, his remains were transferred home to Cordoba for burial in the family cemetery—a procession famously witnessed by the young Andalusian mystic Ibn Arabi.

  • Key Point: Ibn Rushd passed away in Marrakesh on 10 December 1198 CE before his body was returned to Cordoba.

Impact & Historical Legacy

Ibn Rushd's intellectual reach bridged two civilizations. Within the Islamic world, Bidayat al-Mujtahid remains a foundational text of comparative Sunni jurisprudence. In Western Europe, Latin translations of his Aristotelian commentaries by Michael Scot earned him the title The Commentator, deeply shaping Scholastic philosophy at the University of Paris and early Renaissance inquiry.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This biographical account of Ibn Rushd's passing in 595 AH / 1198 CE draws on Imam al-Dhahabi's biographical notices in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' and Almohad-era historical annals in Ibn al-Athir's Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh. Architectural contexts of Almohad Marrakesh and Cordoba are referenced via ArchNet.
1198-wafatnya-ibnu-rusyd.facts:
Date : 10 December 1198 CE / 9 Safar 595 AH
Location : Marrakesh, Morocco (reburied in Cordoba, Andalusia)
Key Figures : Ibn Rushd (Averroes), Caliph Abu Ya'qub Yusuf, Caliph Ya'qub al-Mansur
Major Works : Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Al-Kulliyyat fi al-Tibb, Fasl al-Maqal, Tahafut al-Tahafut
Significance : Chief judge and polymath whose works shaped Islamic comparative law and European Scholasticism

1219-invasi-mongol-ke-khwarezmia.title: Mongol Invasion of Khwarazmia
1219-invasi-mongol-ke-khwarezmia.summary: Between 1219 and 1221 CE, Genghis Khan's Mongol armies invaded the Khwarazmian Empire, devastating major Islamic centers including Bukhara, Samarkand, and Merv.
1219-invasi-mongol-ke-khwarezmia.body:
Context & Background

By the early thirteenth century, as Great Seljuk authority faded, the Khwarazmian Empire under Shah Ala ad-Din Muhammad II dominated Transoxiana, Khurasan, and Iran from the Syr Darya to Iraq's frontier. Eastward, Temujin—proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206—united the Mongol tribes, subjugated northern Jin China, and annexed Qara Khitai to border Khwarazmia. Seeking commercial ties, Genghis Khan dispatched a 450-merchant caravan to Otrar in 1218. However, Otrar's governor Inalchuq accused the traders of espionage, seized their goods, and executed them; Shah Muhammad subsequently killed the Mongol envoy demanding restitution, triggering full-scale invasion.

Course of Events

1. Crossing the Syr Darya and Fall of Bukhara and Samarkand (1219–1220 CE)

In autumn 1219 (616 AH), Genghis Khan crossed the Syr Darya with an army of roughly 100,000–150,000 horsemen backed by Chinese siege engineers. Rather than massing his forces, Shah Muhammad dispersed garrisons into walled cities. Splitting into four columns, Mongol forces besieged Otrar while Genghis Khan marched across the Kyzylkum Desert to strike behind Khwarazmian lines. Bukhara fell in February 1220, followed by Samarkand in March 1220. Shah Muhammad fled westward across Persia and died on a Caspian Sea island late in 1220.

  • Key Point: Splitting Mongol columns and crossing the Kyzylkum Desert allowed Genghis Khan to capture Bukhara and Samarkand within two months.

2. Devastation of Khurasan, Merv, and Urgench (1221 CE)

While Mongol generals Jebe and Subutai pursued the Shah across Iran, Genghis Khan's youngest son Tolui Khan campaigned across Khurasan in 1221 (618 AH). Great centers of learning and commerce—Merv, Nishapur, and Herat—suffered systematic destruction; populations were led outside the walls for slaughter, artisans deported to Mongolia, and ancient libraries lost. Concurrently, the capital Gurganj (Urgench) fell after fierce street fighting and flooding from breached Amu Darya dams.

  • Key Point: Tolui Khan's 1221 campaign devastated Merv, Nishapur, and Urgench along with their scholarly libraries and agricultural infrastructure.

3. Jalal al-Din Mingburnu's Stand at the Indus

Shah Muhammad's son, Jalal al-Din Mingburnu, mounted a stubborn resistance in Afghanistan, defeating a Mongol vanguard at Parwan in 1221. Genghis Khan personally cornered him on the Indus River in November 1221; Jalal al-Din leaped on horseback into the river and escaped into India, ending organized Khwarazmian defense.

  • Key Point: Defeat at the Indus River in November 1221 ended organized Khwarazmian military resistance.

Impact & Historical Legacy

The invasion inflicted immense demographic and urban ruin across Central Asia and Iran, destroying underground qanat irrigation networks across arid plains. Contemporary historian Ibn al-Athir recorded the calamity as unprecedented in human history. Waves of displaced scholars and artisans—including the family of poet Jalal al-Din Rumi—migrated westward to Anatolia, Syria, and India, while Mongol supremacy in Iran laid the groundwork for Hulagu Khan's sack of Baghdad in 1258.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This history of the 616–618 AH / 1219–1221 CE Mongol invasion draws on Ibn al-Athir's contemporary eyewitness account in Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh and Imam al-Dhahabi's historical chronicles in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'. Architectural heritage of Bukhara, Samarkand, and Merv is referenced via ArchNet.
1219-invasi-mongol-ke-khwarezmia.facts:
Date : 1219–1221 CE / 616–618 AH
Location : Transoxiana and Khurasan (Otrar, Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv, Nishapur)
Key Figures : Genghis Khan, Tolui Khan, Shah Ala ad-Din Muhammad II, Jalal al-Din Mingburnu
Parties Involved : Mongol Empire vs Khwarazmian Empire
Significance : Destruction of eastern Islamic urban and scholarly centers and onset of Mongol rule over Central Asia and Iran

1258-jatuhnya-baghdad.title: The Fall of Baghdad
1258-jatuhnya-baghdad.summary: Mongol forces under Hulagu Khan captured and devastated Baghdad in February 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate in Iraq.
1258-jatuhnya-baghdad.body:
Context & Background

By the mid-thirteenth century CE, the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad exercised direct authority only over central and southern Iraq, while military power across the Islamic world was divided among regional sultanates. Caliph al-Musta'sim Billah (r. 1242–1258 CE) struggled with fiscal deficits, sectarian friction between Sunni and Shi'i quarters in the capital, and a depleted standing garrison resulting from troop reductions.

To the east, Great Khan Möngke dispatched his brother Hulagu Khan on a major campaign to subdue Iran, Iraq, and Syria. After dismantling the Nizari Ismaili fortresses around Alamut in 1256 CE, Hulagu massed his forces on the Iranian plateau and sent an ultimatum demanding that al-Musta'sim demolish Baghdad's fortifications and submit as a tributary. Al-Musta'sim's refusal without adequate military mobilization triggered a full-scale siege in early 1258 CE.

Course of Events

1. Encirclement Across the Tigris

  • Key Point: Mongol contingents under Hulagu on the east bank and Baiju on the west bank encircled Baghdad in mid-January 1258 CE.

An Abbasid vanguard of roughly 20,000 soldiers attempted to block Baiju's advance west of the Tigris, but Mongol engineers breached river dikes and flooded the Baghdad camp. On 29 January 1258 CE, Hulagu's troops dug siege trenches around the perimeter walls and deployed siege engines against the eastern Ajami Tower.

2. Breach of the Eastern Wall and Surrender

  • Key Point: Baghdad's eastern ramparts collapsed in early February 1258 CE, compelling Caliph al-Musta'sim to surrender on 10 February 1258 CE.

After a week of sustained bombardment, Mongol assault teams seized the eastern fortifications between 4 and 5 February 1258 CE. Diplomatic overtures led by vizier Ibn al-Alqami failed to halt the assault because Hulagu insisted on unconditional capitulation. On 10 February 1258 CE (4 Safar 656 AH), Caliph al-Musta'sim exited the city with his sons and senior officials to Hulagu's camp.

3. Sack of the City and Execution of the Caliph

  • Key Point: Beginning on 13 February 1258 CE, Mongol forces plundered Baghdad for seven days, destroying major mosques, palaces, and manuscript libraries.

Hulagu ordered a systematic sack and massacre of the city's inhabitants, sparing Nestorian Christians at the request of his wife Doquz Khatun along with select dignitaries. The caliphal palaces, the Mosque of al-Mansur, the Nizamiyya Madrasa, and major manuscript repositories suffered severe destruction and fire. On 20 February 1258 CE (14 Safar 656 AH), Caliph al-Musta'sim and most of his male heirs were executed outside the city.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The fall of Baghdad ended more than five centuries of Abbasid rule in Iraq dating back to 750 CE. Political and scholarly leadership in the Sunni Islamic world shifted westward to Cairo under the Mamluk Sultanate, which installed Ahmad al-Mustansir as a ceremonial Abbasid caliph in 1261 CE.

Although the devastation crippled Mesopotamia's ancient canal networks and killed vast numbers of residents, significant portions of Baghdad's scientific heritage survived elsewhere. The astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi transferred thousands of manuscripts to the Maragheh Observatory in Iran, while displaced scholars in Damascus and Cairo preserved classical Islamic curricula for subsequent generations.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This account draws upon the fourteenth-century chronicle Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela) by Ibn Kathir for the Safar 656 AH sequence of events, the pre-1258 urban geography recorded in Mu'jam al-Buldan (Shamela) by Yaqut al-Hamawi, and architectural heritage records in ArchNet. Troop strengths and casualty figures in medieval chronicles represent traditional estimates rather than modern census counts.
1258-jatuhnya-baghdad.facts:
Year : 656 AH / January–February 1258 CE
Location : Baghdad, Tigris River Valley (Iraq)
Key Figures : Caliph al-Musta'sim Billah, Hulagu Khan, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Ibn al-Alqami
Besieging Force : Ilkhanate Mongol army and allied contingents
Outcome : Execution of Caliph al-Musta'sim on 20 February 1258 CE; end of the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad

1260-pertempuran-ain-jalut.title: The Battle of Ain Jalut
1260-pertempuran-ain-jalut.summary: Mamluk forces from Egypt led by Qutuz and Baybars defeated the Mongol army in Palestine on 3 September 1260, halting their westward advance.
1260-pertempuran-ain-jalut.body:
Context & Background

Following the sack of Baghdad in 1258 CE, Hulagu Khan's army crossed the Euphrates, captured Aleppo and Damascus in early 1260 CE, and threatened Egypt. Mongol envoys delivered an ultimatum to Cairo demanding unconditional submission from the Mamluk Sultanate. Sultan Sayf al-Din Qutuz rejected the demand and executed the envoys, committing Egypt to open war.

In mid-1260 CE, Hulagu withdrew eastward with the bulk of his army upon learning of Great Khan Möngke's death, leaving an occupying force of roughly 10,000 to 20,000 troops in Syria under his Nestorian Christian general, Kitbuqa Noyan. Seizing the strategic opening, Qutuz reconciled with his rival Rukn al-Din Baybars of the Bahri Mamluks and marched Egypt's field army northeast into Palestine.

Course of Events

1. Coastal March and Crusader Neutrality

  • Key Point: Mamluk forces marched along the Palestinian coast after securing neutral passage and supplies from the Crusader authorities at Acre.

In July 1260 CE, the Mamluk army advanced through Gaza, where Baybars's vanguard drove off a Mongol reconnaissance detachment. Advancing northward past Acre, Qutuz obtained an agreement of neutrality and logistical provisioning from the Crusader barons, enabling the Mamluk cavalry to pivot inland into Galilee without risking a flank attack.

2. Feigned Retreat in the Jezreel Valley

  • Key Point: On 3 September 1260 CE, Baybars lured Kitbuqa's heavy cavalry into an ambush encircled by the main Mamluk force.

The two armies met at dawn on 25 Ramadan 658 AH (3 September 1260 CE) near the spring of Ain Jalut. Qutuz concealed the main Mamluk divisions along the surrounding hills while Baybars engaged the Mongol vanguard with hit-and-run volleys before feigning retreat. Kitbuqa committed his entire cavalry force in pursuit, riding directly into the valley basin.

3. Qutuz's Counterattack and Mongol Collapse

  • Key Point: When the Mamluk left flank buckled, Qutuz led a personal countercharge that broke the Mongol formation and resulted in Kitbuqa's capture.

An intense Mongol cavalry assault initially threatened to shatter the Mamluk left wing. Qutuz threw off his helmet so his troops could recognize him, cried out "Wa Islamah!" (O Islam!), and led the reserve down the slopes. Surrounded on three sides, the Mongol force broke; Kitbuqa was captured and executed on the field, while retreating units were routed near Baysan.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The victory at Ain Jalut permanently halted the westward military expansion of the Mongol Empire into Egypt and North Africa. Within weeks of the battle, Mamluk forces retook Damascus, Hama, Homs, and Aleppo, pushing surviving Mongol garrisons back across the Euphrates River.

Geopolitically, the Mamluk Sultanate established itself as the foremost Islamic power protecting Egypt, Syria, and the Two Holy Sanctuaries of the Hijaz for more than two and a half centuries until 1517 CE. The battle also propelled Baybars to the sultanate later in 1260 CE, initiating decades of Syrian fortification and scholarly patronage in Cairo and Damascus.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This narrative relies on the 658 AH annals in Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela) by Ibn Kathir, biographical accounts of contemporary figures in Siyar A'lam an-Nubala' (Shamela) by al-Dhahabi, and the geographical entry for Ain Jalut in Mu'jam al-Buldan (Shamela). Exact troop numbers differ across Mamluk and Persian chronicles.
1260-pertempuran-ain-jalut.facts:
Year : 25 Ramadan 658 AH / 3 September 1260 CE
Location : Ain Jalut, Jezreel Valley, Palestine
Mamluk Commanders : Sultan Sayf al-Din Qutuz and Rukn al-Din Baybars
Mongol Commander : Kitbuqa Noyan
Result : Decisive Mamluk victory; the Euphrates River stabilized as the western Ilkhanate frontier

1297-wafatnya-sultan-malik-as-saleh-samu.title: Death of Sultan Malik al-Saleh of Samudra Pasai
1297-wafatnya-sultan-malik-as-saleh-samu.summary: The tombstone of Sultan Malik al-Saleh in Aceh, dated 696 AH (1297 CE), stands as the oldest dated epigraphic evidence of an Islamic sultanate in the Malay-Indonesian archipelago.
1297-wafatnya-sultan-malik-as-saleh-samu.body:
Context & Background

During the thirteenth century CE, the northern coast of Sumatra emerged as a major Indian Ocean maritime hub linking merchants from Gujarat, Persia, Arabia, and China. Situated near the mouth of the Pasai River, the Sultanate of Samudra Pasai developed into the earliest documented Islamic kingdom in the Indonesian archipelago with dated royal epigraphy.

According to the Malay chronicle Hikayat Raja-raja Pasai, a local ruler named Meurah Silu embraced Islam through scholarly and diplomatic contacts with envoys linked to Mecca and coastal Muslim teachers, adopting the regnal title Sultan Malik al-Saleh. Contemporary outside corroboration appears in the travel account of Marco Polo, who anchored along northern Sumatra in 1292 CE and noted established Muslim communities in Perlak and neighboring ports.

Course of Events

1. Consolidation of the North Sumatran Port Polity

  • Key Point: Sultan Malik al-Saleh united the settlements of Samudra and Pasai and organized maritime trade regulations along the Strait of Malacca.

Under Malik al-Saleh, Samudra Pasai leveraged its sheltered anchorage along the Strait of Malacca to export pepper, camphor, and gold. The court combined Shafi'i Islamic jurisprudence with coastal Malay customary law and reinforced its regional legitimacy through marriage into the ruling house of Perlak.

2. Passing of the Sultan in 696 AH

  • Key Point: Sultan Malik al-Saleh died in Ramadan 696 AH (1297 CE), as inscribed in Arabic calligraphy on his surviving funerary stele.

The carved stone monument preserved at Gampong Beuringen in North Aceh records the death of the ruler in the month of Ramadan, year 696 AH (corresponding to 1297 CE). Carved in Naskhi-Thuluth script, the stele bears Qur'anic verses alongside Sufi poetry reflecting on human mortality.

3. Succession of Sultan Muhammad Malik al-Zahir

  • Key Point: The throne passed peacefully to his son, Sultan Muhammad Malik al-Zahir (r. 1297–1326 CE), who introduced gold dirham coinage.

Following his father's death, Sultan Muhammad Malik al-Zahir expanded Pasai's political reach across Pidie and northeastern Sumatra. Gold dirham coins minted in Pasai circulated widely as trusted currency across Southeast Asian spice networks.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The tombstone of Sultan Malik al-Saleh serves as the oldest securely dated archaeological proof of an Islamic sultanate in Nusantara, predating surviving royal Islamic inscriptions in Java by roughly a century and a half. Its stone carving motifs indicate artistic and commercial ties connecting Gujarati workshops in Cambay with Sumatran artisans.

As a pioneering Islamic center, Samudra Pasai fostered Malay-language religious scholarship in Jawi script and trained scholars whose networks later extended to Malacca, Java, and Patani. The 696 AH inscription remains the foundational chronological anchor for Southeast Asian Islamic historiography.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

This entry cross-references the 696 AH/1297 CE funerary epigraphy with classical Malay literary sources such as Hikayat Raja-raja Pasai preserved in Khastara Perpusnas RI and Nusantara religious manuscript catalogs at Lektur Kemenag RI. While historians debate the exact year of Malik al-Saleh's conversion, his death date in Ramadan 696 AH is directly attested on the surviving stone monument.
1297-wafatnya-sultan-malik-as-saleh-samu.facts:
Year : Ramadan 696 AH / 1297 CE
Location : Geudong, Samudra Pasai, North Aceh (Indonesia)
Ruler : Sultan Malik al-Saleh (Meurah Silu)
Material Evidence : Arabic-inscribed tombstone dated 696 AH at Gampong Beuringen
Successor : Sultan Muhammad Malik al-Zahir

1299-awal-berdirinya-kesultanan-utsmani.title: Founding of the Ottoman Emirate
1299-awal-berdirinya-kesultanan-utsmani.summary: Osman I established an autonomous frontier principality in northwestern Anatolia around 1299 CE that grew into the Ottoman Empire.
1299-awal-berdirinya-kesultanan-utsmani.body:
Context & Background

By the closing decade of the thirteenth century CE, the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia had fragmented under Mongol Ilkhanate overlordship following its defeat at Köse Dağ in 1243 CE. The collapse of central authority produced more than a dozen autonomous Turkish principalities (beyliks) across western Anatolia along the Byzantine frontier.

One small beylik was led by Ertuğrul of the Kayı clan, centered in the pastures of Söğüt and Domaniç. Upon Ertuğrul's death around 1280 CE, leadership passed to his son Osman I, who cultivated close ties with frontier warriors (ghazis), the Ahi urban guilds, and local religious scholars including Shaykh Edebali.

Course of Events

1. Assertion of Autonomy in Bithynia

  • Key Point: Around 1299 CE, Osman I captured Bilecik, Yarhisar, and İnegöl and asserted autonomous authority in northwestern Anatolia.

Weakening Byzantine control over Bithynia enabled Osman I to capture Karacahisar (1288–1291 CE) and subsequently seize Bilecik and Yarhisar in 1299 CE. According to Ottoman chronicle tradition, the Friday sermon (khutba) was read in Osman's name by Judge Dursun Fakih at Karacahisar, signaling political independence from declining Seljuk oversight.

2. Victory at Bapheus and Military Consolidation

  • Key Point: On 27 July 1302 CE, Osman's forces defeated a Byzantine imperial army at Bapheus (Koyunhisar), establishing Ottoman primacy in Bithynia.

The victory at Bapheus demonstrated the Ottoman emirate's ability to defeat regular Byzantine field forces. News of the triumph drew Turkish volunteers from central Anatolia to Osman's standard, tightening the blockade around major Byzantine walled cities such as Nicaea (İznik) and Bursa.

3. Administrative Foundations and the Capture of Bursa

  • Key Point: Before his death around 1324–1326 CE, Osman established early fiscal policies that enabled his son Orhan to capture Bursa in 1326 CE.

Osman I levied moderate taxes on submitted Greek agrarian communities and protected trade routes leading toward the Sea of Marmara. As command passed to his son Orhan during Osman's final years, Ottoman forces compelled Bursa to surrender on 6 April 1326 CE, turning it into the dynasty's first major capital.

Historical Impact & Legacy

The principality founded around Söğüt in 1299 CE evolved into the Ottoman Empire, the longest-lived Islamic imperial state, enduring for more than six centuries until 1922 CE. From a modest frontier emirate in Bithynia, Ottoman armies crossed the Dardanelles into the Balkans in the mid-fourteenth century and conquered Constantinople in 1453 CE.

Institutionally, the synthesis of Oghuz steppe traditions, classical Islamic governance, and pragmatic frontier administration laid down under Osman and Orhan formed a durable multi-ethnic state encompassing Anatolia, the Balkans, Syria, Egypt, and the Hijaz.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

Contemporary fourteenth-century Syrian awareness of rising Turkish frontier emirates bordering Byzantine territory appears in Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela) by Ibn Kathir, while early Ottoman civic and religious architecture in Bursa and Iznik is cataloged in ArchNet. Modern historians note that 1299 CE reflects fifteenth-century Ottoman chronicle convention alongside the securely dated 1302 CE victory at Bapheus.
1299-awal-berdirinya-kesultanan-utsmani.facts:
Year : c. 1299 CE (698–699 AH)
Location : Söğüt and Bilecik, Northwestern Anatolia (Turkey)
Founder : Osman I (Osman ibn Ertuğrul)
Political Context : Fragmentation of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum into Anatolian Beyliks
Initial Base : Bithynian frontier facing the Byzantine Empire

1325-ibnu-battuta-memulai-pengembaraanny.title: Ibn Battuta Begins His Travels
1325-ibnu-battuta-memulai-pengembaraanny.summary: Ibn Battuta departed Tangier in June 1325 CE to perform the pilgrimage to Mecca and went on to travel across the Islamic world and beyond for nearly three decades.
1325-ibnu-battuta-memulai-pengembaraanny.body:
Context & Background

In the early fourteenth century CE, the Islamic world was linked by overland caravan corridors and maritime sea lanes stretching from the Atlantic coast of Morocco to the South China Sea. Although political authority was divided among the Marinid Sultanate in the Maghrib, the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt and Syria, the Ilkhanate in Persia, the Delhi Sultanate in India, and coastal Southeast Asian polities, shared Arabic legal scholarship facilitated movement for jurists and travelers.

Born in Tangier on 24 February 1304 CE into a family of Maliki jurists, Shams al-Din Ibn Battuta received a formal legal education in his youth. At age twenty-one, he set out to perform the pilgrimage to Mecca while studying under leading scholars in Egypt and Syria.

Course of Events

1. Departure from Tangier to Mecca

  • Key Point: Ibn Battuta departed Tangier alone on 14 June 1325 CE (2 Rajab 725 AH) riding a donkey along the North African coast.

His initial itinerary passed through Tlemcen, Bejaia, and Tunis, where he joined a pilgrim caravan as a traveling qadi to settle disputes. He reached Alexandria in April 1326 CE, visited Mamluk Cairo under Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, and traveled overland through Damascus and Medina to complete his first Hajj in Mecca in late 1326 CE.

2. Journeys Across Central Asia, India, and Southeast Asia

  • Key Point: Rather than returning home after the pilgrimage, Ibn Battuta toured Iraq, Persia, Anatolia, and the Kipchak Steppe before serving eight years as a judge in Delhi.

In Constantinople, he met Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos before crossing Central Asia through Bukhara and Samarkand. Arriving in India around 1333 CE, Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq appointed him Maliki qadi of Delhi and later dispatched him as an envoy to the Yuan court in China via Malabar, the Maldives, Bengal, and Samudra Pasai.

3. Return to Fez and Compilation of the Rihla

  • Key Point: After visiting al-Andalus and the Mali Empire in West Africa, Ibn Battuta dictated his travel account to Ibn Juzayy in Fez in 1355 CE.

Ibn Battuta returned to Morocco in 1349 CE amid the Black Death, yet still traveled to Granada and crossed the Sahara to Timbuktu and Mali between 1352 and 1353 CE. At the command of Marinid Sultan Abu Inan Faris, he dictated his twenty-nine-year itinerary to court scribe Ibn Juzayy al-Kalbi in Tuhfat al-Nuzzar fi Ghara'ib al-Amsar wa Aja'ib al-Asfar.

Historical Impact & Legacy

Covering an estimated 117,000 kilometers, Ibn Battuta's travels surpassed those of any other known medieval traveler, including Marco Polo. His Rihla remains an indispensable primary source on urban society, Islamic courts, Sufi lodges, maritime trade goods, and Muslim communities across West Africa, Anatolia, India, and Southeast Asia in the fourteenth century.

Through firsthand observation of royal courts and port cities, his account demonstrates the institutional mobility of Islamic legal culture, allowing a North African jurist to hold judicial office in India and the Maldives.

Methodology Note (About This Telling)

The Mamluk cities and Syrian-Egyptian political setting observed by Ibn Battuta between 1325 and 1350 CE are corroborated by the contemporary chronicle Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah (Shamela) by Ibn Kathir, urban geography in Mu'jam al-Buldan (Shamela), and architectural documentation of Marinid and Mamluk monuments in ArchNet. Historians note that portions of his East Asian chronology were edited by Ibn Juzayy from memory after original notes were lost en route.
1325-ibnu-battuta-memulai-pengembaraanny.facts:
Year : 2 Rajab 725 AH / 14 June 1325 CE – 1354 CE
Departure Point : Tangier, Marinid Sultanate (Morocco)
Traveler : Shams al-Din Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Battuta
